Mr. Thomas Vien (Lotlbiniere) presented the tenth report of the select standing committee on Banking and Commerce as follows:
Pursuant to the Order of Reference from this House of the 31st of March, 1924, your committee, in view of the failure of the Home Bank, have considered the provisions of the Bank Act with a view to recommending such amendments to the act as would better protect the interests of bank depositors generally, and would prevent similar occurrences in the future:
And your committee are of the opinion that it is expedient to bring in a measure to amend the Bank Act and they therefore recommend that the said act be amended as follows:
That Section 56A of the Bank Act be repealed, and the following substituted therefor:
' 'Inspection:
"56A. 1. The Governor in Council on the recommendation of the minister shall appoint a person who in his opinion has had proper training and experience who shall be charged with the performance of the duties hereinafter mentioned. Such person shall be designated "Inpector General of Banks". The minister may direct some other such person to temporarily perform the duties of the inspector should the inspector, by reason of illness or other contingency, be unable to perform such duties.
"2. The Inspector shall hold office during good behaviour, but may be removed from office by the Governor in Council for misbehaviour or incapacity, inability, or failure to perform his duties properly.
"3. If the Inspector is removed from office for any such reason the order in council providing for such

Banking and Commerce-Report
removal and documents relating thereto shall be laid before parliament within the first fifteen days of the next ensuing session.
"4. The Inspector while holding office shall not perform any service for compensation other than the service rendered by him under the provisions of this section.
"5. The minister may appoint or employ on the recommendation of the Deputy Minister of Finance and the inspector, such persons with training and experience and such clerical assistants as may be deemed necessary to carry out and give effect to the provisions of this section. Persons so appointed or employed shall receive such salary or remuneration as may be fixed by the minister".
" 6. The inspector, from time to time, but not less frequently than once in each calendar year shall make or cause to be made, such examination and inquiry into the affairs or business of each bank as he may deem to be necessary or expedient, and for such purposes to take charge of the assets of the bank or any portion thereof, if the need should arise for the purpose of satisfying himself that the provisions of this act have reference to the safety of the creditors and shareholders of each such bank are being duly observed and that the bank is in a sound financial condition. The inspector at the conclusion of each such examination and inquiry shall report thereon to the minister.
" 7. A copy of all reports made by the auditors of a bank to the general manager and to the directors under the next preceding section shall be transmitted or delivered to the minister by the auditors at the same time as such reports are transmitted or delivered to the general manager and directors.
" 8. The inspector, or person acting under his direction, shall have a right of access to the books and accounts, documents, vouchers and securities of the bank, and shall be entitled to require and receive from the directors, officers and auditors of the bank such information and explanation as he may deem necessary for the performance of his duties.
9. The inspector shall have all the powers conferred upon a commissioner appointed under the Inquiries Act for the purpose of obtaining evidence under oath, and may delegate such powers as occasion may require. Any person who refuses to give such evidence or to produce any book or document material thereto when required so to do shall be guilty of an offence against this act.
"10. Whenever the inspector is satisfied that a bank is insolvent he shall report fully on the bank's condition to the minister and the minister may, without waiting for the bank to suspend payment in specie or Dominion notes of any of its liabilities as they accrue, request the association or the president of the association to appoint a curator to supervise the affairs of such bank, and such request shall have the same effect as if the bank had suspended payment in specie or Dominion notes of any of its liabilities as they accrued, and a curator shall forthwith be appointed as provided in section 117 of this act.
"11. The inspector shall be paid a salary fixed by the Governor in Council on the recommendation of the minister.
" 12. All salaries, remunerations and other expenses incidental to giving effect to this section shall be paid out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund, and the Consolidated Revenue Fund shall be recouped after the end of each calendar year for such outlay by an assessment upon the banks based upon the average total assets of the banks respectively during the year, as shown by the monthly returns made by the banks to the minister under section 112, and such assessment shall be paid by the banks.
"13. All persons appointed under this section shall be officers of the Department of Finance, but the 
provisions of the Civil Service Act, 1918, shall not apply to such persons.
" 14. Any bank or any director, president, general manager or any officer of a bank who directly or indirectly makes a loan or grant or gives any gratuity to the inspector or any other person appointed or employed under this section and the inspector or any such person who accepts or receives directly or indirectly, any such loan, grant or gratuity, commits an offence against this act, and is liable as provided in section 157 of this Act, in addition to any punishment otherwise provided.
" 15. The inspector or any person appointed or employed under this section who disclose to any other person, except the Minister and the Deputy Minister of Finance, any information regarding a bank, its business or affairs commits an offence against this act and is liable as provided in section 157 of the act.
" 16. Provided, however, that the government shall not incur any liability whatever to any depositor, creditor or shareholder of any bank, or to any other person, for any damages, payment, compensation or indemnity which he may suffer or claim by reason of this section or anything therein contained, or by reason of anything done or omitted to be done under the requirements thereof, or by reason of anything omitted to be done which is hereby required to be done, or by reason of any order or direction of the Governor in Council or of the minister in the execution or administration of the powers or any or them by this section conferred, or by reason of any failure or omission on the part of governor in council or of the minister or of the inspector or of any officer or employee of the government to execute or discharge any power, authority or duty thereunder, or otherwise by reason of any default, negligence, mistake, error or omission in the administration or discharge of the powers or duties which in any circumstances are by this section intended or authorized to be executed or performed; and no such payment, damages, compensation or indemnity, nor any claim therefor, shall in any case be authorized, paid or entertained by the government.
" 17. This section shall come into force on the first day of October, nineteen hundred and twenty-four, but it shall not be incumbent upon the inspector to examine all of the banks under the section during the calendar year one thousand nine hundred and twenty-four."

Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Minister of Justice) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 197 to amend the Winding-up Act.
He said: Under section 34 of the Winding-up Act the liquidator may, with the approval of the court, sell any real and personal property belonging to the bankrupt estate and transfer it to any person or company. The amendment proposes to add the words, "for such consideration as may be approved by the court." The purpose is to remove doubts as to the power of the court to approve of the consideration when such consideration is other than cash or equivalent to cash.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

I have received the fo
lowing letter from the Editor of Debates:
June 20, 1924
The Honourable the Speaker.
Sir,-I assume that your announcement in the House that you would call the attention of the chief of the Hansard staff to complaints of discrepancies, is a command to me to report upon the matter. I have the honour, therefore, to submit the following:-
The point to which Mr. Stewart (Humboldt) called attention is that certain items of the estimates, passed in Committee of Supply, and so recorded in the Votes and Proceedings, are not recorded in Hansard.
The notes of our reporters show that these item were passed without debate. In leaving such item unrecorded in Hansard, the reporters followed instruc tions given them, which instructions, so far as I knov have stood unchanged ever since Hansard was estafc lished.
As this may seem to call for explanation, I sub mb further: It has always been assumed that the work of Hansard was limited to recording debates, the verj title of our service-" Official Report of Debates "-indicating the bounds of our territory. Of course, certain items of the proceedings must be recorded also in order to make the report of debates intelligible, but we have never supposed that Hansard would be looked to as a record of proceedings.
Our reporters, and all of us who are engaged in the work of Hansard, are most desirous of performing our whole duty in the honourable positions we hold as servants of the House of Commons of Canada. In this case to which attention has been called, we followed what to us is immemorial custom, based, we assume, upon instructions originally given by competent authority.
I have the honour to be, Sir,
Your obedient servant,
A. C. Campbell
Editor of Debates.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
I desire, with all respect, to refer to the statement made by Your

Votes and Proceedings and Hansard
Honour, and the letter which has been read from the Speaker's chair. I have the utmost respect for the Editor of Debates, but I have not so understood the purpose of Hansard, and I think it is an error if Hansard is continued on that principle. The letter of the Editor of Debates was designed to prove that Hansard was merely a record of debates as between one member and another of this House, and not as well a record of all the proceedings of the House, inclusive of statements by Your Honour and of motions passed without debate as read from the chair. I just turned up a Hansard which was on my desk, and I give this only by way of illustration. At page 3829 of the Hansard of last year, June 13, I find the following:
Royal Assent
A message was delivered by Colonel Ernest J'. Chambers, Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod, as follows:
Mr. Speaker, His Honour the Deputy of His Excellency the Governor General desires the immediate attendance of this honourable House in the Chamber of the Honourable the Senate.
Accordingly, the House went up to the Senate.
And having returned,
Mr. Speaker informed the House that the Deputy of His Excellency the Governor General had been pleased to give in His Majesty's name the Royal Assent to the following bills.
Then follow two and a half columns of bills that had been assented to. Thereupon there is no debate, and the next item is Supply. This clearly shows that Hansard is much more than a record of	debates, it
is a record of proceedings; and I think should be a complete record of proceedings. In this connection let me urge, or at least let me suggest, that if Hansard were a complete record of proceedings, which it certainly is, save to a very slight extent, and I think should be fully-this illustration shows it has been a record of more than debates-then really, I do not see what object is served by the Votes and Proceedings publication.	A very great economy could be
effected by abolishing the Votes and Proceed-ngs publication altogether. All that is ever left out of Hansard is little, and I did not know there was anything intentionally left out, and I urge strongly there should be nothing. Let us have one record, and let that record be complete.

This morning I had a
risit from the Editor of Debates, Mr. Campbell, who is an old and trusted official who has served the House of Commons for almost thirty-five years, and he states that from time immemorial the debates have been reported as they are reported to-day. It so happens that at times items are carried with-
out any debate at all, and Mr. Campbell says that his understanding has always been, and his instructions from the Debates committee have always been, that the reporters of his staff shall report only the debates. I must say to the House that if they have any other instructions to give to our very able staff of Hansard reporters the matter should be referred to the Debates committee. The Debates committee does not meet very often, but it should meet on such an occasion at least.
Now as regards the Votes and Proceedings, which constitute the official record of what takes place before the House, let me read from Bourinot at page 182, speaking of the officers of the House of Commons and their duties, he says:
The clerk of the House is its recording officer, appointed by the Crown under the great seal of Canada and holds office during pleasure, virtually until his health or age no longer permits him to perform his duties. He has also, by the terms of the Civil Service Act, the rank of deputy minister, and in the operation of that act is charged with special duties and functions with respect to clerkships of the staff of the House. He takes notes of the proceedings of the Commons without any reference to the debate. He is "to make entries, remembrances, and journals of the things done and passed in the House of Commons; but it is without warrant that he should make minutes of particular men's speeches". His minutes, technically styled "the scroll", are made up every day in a brief and convenient shape, known as the "votes and proceedings," which comprise a record of all the proceedings, but omit many of the parliamentary forms which are given in full in the journals, when these are extended after the close of a session. He signs the orders of the House, endorses addresses and bills sent or returned to the Senate and reads whatever is required to be read in the House.
This shows that the Votes and Proceedings and the Scroll constitute the authentic record of what takes place in the House. But if it is the desire of the House, as suggested by the right hon. leader of the opposition, that Hansard should report what from time immemorial until to-day, Mr. Campbell states, has never been reported, that is items that are passed without any debate, it is for the House to instruct the Debates committee accordingly. I am informed by Mr. Campbell that he would accept the directions of the House in the matter. He is a very able and trusted official of the House of Commons.
What duty or function has the committee of Debates to perform?

Such matters as are referred to it by the House of Commons concerning the report of debates, the qualifications of the Hansard reporters, and matters generally concerning the official report of evidence before committees.

Votes and Proceedings and Hansard

I have been a member
of that committee for the last two or three years, but I do not remember a meeting having been held.

Possibly it is because as a matter of fact-and I am very sincere-the reports of the proceedings of the House by our Hansard staff are creditable to the country and to the House. I think I may say that.

speakeroldname: Mr. T. W. CALDWELL (Victoria and Car-leton):
speechtext:
I am sure, Mr. Speaker, there was
no thought in the mind of any members in the House to reflect either upon the Editor of Debates or upon the reporting staff of the House when this question was raised yesterday. I have been a member of this House for a number of years and this is the first time it has been called to my attention that items of Supply are treated differently when they are debated and when they are not. I can hardly understand why there should be any difference in the method of reporting in connection with the calling of an item when it is debated and when it is not. The saving effected in not reporting the items called and passed without debate would be infinitesimal. If the committee would rule that the debates on some of these estimates should not be reported, I think that condition might be justified; it seems to me that in some cases a good part of the discussion might be cut out. For instance, we find on page 3438 of yesterday's Hansard, to illustrate what I mean, the following item:
Honorary Advisory Council of Scientific and Industrial Research, $120,000.
If this item had not been discussed it would appear in that form and the only additional words would be, "Item agreed to." I would certainly recommend that the method be changed, and I say that without any desire to reflect upon the Editor of Debates, for whom I have the highest respect both for h'v ability and for his thoughtful care over the new members of the House-as we all were once. I am sure there is no thought of reflecting upon him in any way.
I am sure that the Hansard reporters will take heed of the remarks made this afternoon and that it will not require even the calling of the Debates committee to have that little reform instituted.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
In justice to the present staff of
reporters, Mr. Speaker, I must say that I have been a member of this House for over twenty years, and this is not the first time it has come to my notice that when items in the estimates 219
are carried without discussion they are not reported in Hansard and that we have to look at the Votes and Proceedings to find them. That has always been the case, and I do not know that we should transform Hansard into an official record of the proceedings of the House. It is rather a report of the discussions for the information of those who desire to know what takes place in the House, but it has never had the character of being as official as some members would like it to be. Perhaps we would all suffer if it were so. It happens that our mistakes in speeches, either in French or in English, are corrected in Hansard, and it is good for all of us; if it were an absolutely official report of what took place many of us would suffer. Perhaps the reporters will view it in that way.

I suggest it might be a
wise thing for the Debates committee to meet and discuss this situation.

I just wish to mention,
because it seems to have been overlooked, that the case to which I called attention shows that the rule has not prevailed.

My long experience in this House enables me to state that Hansard has never been looked upon as an official record of the House. The Votes and Proceedings, transformed into the Journals of the House at the end of each session, and signed by the Speaker, constitute the official record of this House; and if you wish to give evidence in a court of justice as to what really occurred in parliament you must produce this document, not Hansard. The drawback of Hansard is that when you seek information on any particular item which was not discussed in parliament there is a likelihood that no mention of it is made in Hansard, therefore Hansard is deficient in that respect. I think it would be a good thing if all the actions of this House were reported in Hansard, so that this costly publication, the suppression of which has been discussed a dozen times during my experience, should at least be a complete record of the proceedings of parliament. If that were done you w'ould not have to refer back for this information to the journals of the House, a publication which few people possess outside, of members of the House, while on the other hand, Hansard is distributed to the public libraries and generally throughout the country and is easily accessible. As I say, Hansard is deficient in that respect; when there is no debate the reporters are not required to make any mention of the undebated

3458	COMMONS
Votes and Proceedings and Hansard
subject, but for the convenience of the readers of Hansard it seems to me that mention ought to be made of these matters. But if we are to say that Hansard is the official record of parliament we shall have to go back on our present procedure. We had a very stubborn debate on the question here some years ago when the suggestion was made that the French and English journals of the House be combined, making one a mere translation of the other. I think that before any move at all is made in the matter, the Debates committee should meet, as you suggest, Mr. Speaker, discuss all sides of it and then make a recommendation to the House.
Mr. G. H.. BOIVIN (Shefford): It will be a pleasure for me to call the members of the Debates committee together some time next week in order that this matter may be discussed. But I would like to say now that my own opinion agrees very much with that of the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), and that is that Hansard should not be made an official report of the proceedings of this House. I understand that it would be advisable, if possible, to make mention in Hansard of the different votes passed in committee of Supply. Still, if hon. members give the matter a moment's reflection they will see that there are many objections to that plan. The reporter sitting at his table, having the estimates before him as a guide, is obliged to rely upon his hearing and upon the statement made by the Chairman in deciding whether or not a vote or a motion has been passed. Very often an item is called; the minister says "stand," and it is placed to one side. Sometimes a nod of his head to the Chairman is all that takes place and if that item is recorded in Hansard with no notation whatever-if the word "stand" is not used or is not heard by the reporter-then that item appears in Hansard to have been passed.

Does this not apply
to the items that are discussed? The Hansard reporter must depend on his hearing in regard to them.

Absolutely; but when an
item is discussed the Hansard reporter uses the description of the item as it appears in the estimates as a heading for the discussion and the discussion or debate appears in Hansard. Sometimes items are passed after they have been discussed and the fact that the item is carried may not appear in Hansard. Sometimes an item is postponed by unanimous consent, and the fact that it is postponed may 
not be recorded. There is only one man in this House in a position to state whether an item has been passed or not. He holds the responsible position of Assistant Clerk of the House, and sits beside the Chairman of Committees. When an item is passed it is signed by the Chairman of the Committee and is recorded by the Assistant Clerk. From the Assistant Clerk's record the Votes and Proceedings are compiled, and are signed by the Speaker. That record is carefully checked over by three or four officials before it is printed and placed upon each member's desk the following morning as the official record of the proceedings of parliament. If you are going to place upon the Hansard reporters the responsibility of saying whether an item has been passed or not you will sometimes find a contradiction between the Hansard and the Votes and Proceedings and you will have the same trouble now complained of. Every time there happens to be an apparent contradiction there will be more or less confusion; some hon. members will swear by Hansard, and others will rely only upon the Votes and Proceedings. In my opinion there should be only one official record of the proceedings of the House and that should be the Votes and Proceedings.

Do I understand th.
hon. member to say that in no case is the fact that an item is carried after discussion re corded in Hansard?

No. What I said was that
in some cases when items are carried the fact is recorded and in other cases the fact is not recorded. It depends a great deal upon the way in which the item is passed; upon the way in which the next item is read; upon whether two or three items are carried together, or whether they are read separately. It is imposible for the Hansard reporter to give an absolute and faithful report unless a certain course is followed. It would be necessary for the Editor of Hansard to delay publication of the day's debates and obtain from the Clerk of the House official confirmation of the passing of the items. If hon. members wish that to be done it will delay the printing and they will not have Hansard on their desks the following morning at ten o'clock. After a prolonged sitting of the House the report is voluminous and the printing of Hansard is consequently delayed. With the proposed change it would be further delayed and not distributed until three, four oi five o'clock in the afternoon.
Before I take my seat let me add that I would be very glad to have the Debates com-

Postal Employees
mittee consider the suggestion made by the hon. member for Victoria and Carleton (Mr. Caldwell) that discussion in committee be omitted altogether from Hansard. I have often thought that if the reports of the debates were limited to speeches made when the House was sitting with the honourable the Speaker in the chair, and if the reports of debates in Committee of the Whole on a bill, in Supply, or in Ways and Means, were not recorded in Hansard, the rules governing debate would be more strictly adhered to and the sessions of the House would be abridged by at least two months or almost half of their entire duration.

Then we should not
have a repetition of each by-election when items were considered in committee of Supply.

If hon. members deem it
advisable to consider this innovation, it can also be discussed when the Debates committee meets next week and then further debated by hon. members when the ordinary motion is made in connection with the report of the committee which must be presented to the House.
On the Orders of the Day:

Will
the Acting Postmaster General be good enough to state the exact position of the postal controversy at the present time, more particularly with reference to the city of Toronto.

The situation is clearing very rapidly. In Nova Scotia the mails are moving quite normally, there is mo difficulty. The same is true of New Brunswick, of eastern Quebec and Oif Prince Edward Island. Last night in two instances the trains leaving Quebec were not fully manned. They are all fully manned this morning, and Quebec is in a normal condition. In Montreal a considerable number of the regular men are still out on strike. Their positions are being filled very rapidly, and a great many of the employees who went out are coming back. Just before 12 o'clock to-day I had notification that there were five hundred men trying to break into the office to get employment. In the West there has been no disaffection at all. In Hamilton the men returned this morning. We enlisted yesterday about 130 men in that city, but all the strikers returned to duty this morning so that at the 2194
moment we are overmanned in Hamilton. Of course, it is understood that the men who are coming back are returning absolutely without any promise of permanent employment; that is a matter that will have to be adjusted later. WTe are still short of men in Windsor, but as it is not an important distributing point we are not suffering very much inconvenience. I think that in all the smaller post offices in Ontario at 2 o'clock today, with the single exception of Brantford, all the men had returned to work. That statement may not be absolutely correct, but it is a fair summary of the situation. There are about 1,400 men out in Toronto, and in that city we had enlisted yesterday up to midnight about 500 men. At 10 o'clock this morning I issued instructions that no more were to be taken on. I think I can say, with some hope that the statement will be verified that the striking postal employees in Toronto will think better of their action. I have given them until 8 o'clock to-morrow morning to return to duty. If they do not return by that hour they can consider themselves as permanently out of the service.
Was the same concession granted to the striking employees in Montreal?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
It applies
everywhere. The situation in Toronto is that we have been unable to deliver the mails fully to the business houses, but that is to be expected when 1,400 men walk out almost without a moment's notice. We will, we anticipate, be able to move the eastern and western mails to contiguous points and sort them to-day, so that in a couple of days we should be able to restore the movement of the mails to almost a normal condition. In conclusion I wish to say that as Acting Postmaster General I appreciate very much the patience of the public, and the prompt manner in which the business houses and other institutions that are affected rallied to the support of the department and endeavoured to maintain normal conditions in the movement of the mails.
Will the men who have been taken on be protected and retained in the service?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
That is a
very difficult question to answer at the moment; it will require a great deal of thought. All I can say is that very full consideration will be given to the case of the men who have been taken on even in a temporary way.
