maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext:
The hon. member for Brome
(Mr. McMaster) said he thought the present draft was fairly clear but thought that the minister should give way to the suggestion of the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) and allow the matter to stand over for another day, until he could have an opportunity of taking up the matter with the Justice department. It is somewhat encouraging and certainly refreshing, after the long debate Which took place yesterday, to be able to come back to the House and say that the Justice department has borne me out in every interpretation which I have placed on section 12. I refer now to Hansard, and I find that my right hon. friend said:
I should like to get the minister to understand if I could.
This afternoon I will use exactly the same words to the right hon. gentleman (Mr. Meighen) and I say to him, I would like to be able to get the right hon. leader of the opposition to understand, if I could.
This section was first suggested by a reso-

lution by the Canadian Jewellers' Association, assembled in the city of Windsor about a years ago. They submitted a clause which they felt would meet the requirements, and my department sent the clause to the Justice department with instructions to draw up a bill which would meet the requirements. The bill as drawn was sent back to the Justice department this morning, and they inform me that the deputy minister conferred with the assistant deputy minister, and that they decided that the clause was so clear that no ordinary person could misunderstand its meaning. They called in the Deputy Minister of Justice and called in an authority on drafting bills in the department. This gentleman stated that the clause as worded was so clear that he could not see that any change could be made. The clause was inserted in the bill, and, as I said yesterday, it means exactly what it states. Yesterday I stated, in answer to a question of my right hon. friend:
Ninety-five per cent of the whole article represented as platinum.
Again I said:
I think it is ninety-five per cent of the whole article. What value would there be in it if the article might contain ninety-five per cent of other inferior metal?
And the hon. member for Victoria and Carleton (Mr. Caldwell) asked the same question, and I think I replied to him that that was the meaning I gave to it. I understand now, after a further reference to the Justice department, that that is what the bill is intended to cover-that the article must contain ninety-five per cent of platinum. Then again, the object of the jewellers, the people who handle platinum goods in this country, was simply that the word "platinum" should only appear on articles that contained ninety-five per cent platinum. Now with reference to "platinum" and "element platinum," there is practically no difference. The words "element platinum" are used to designate the purest kind of platinum, and these words are inserted in the bill in order to afford the greatest protection possible, this being specially necessary when the metal is to be used for scientific purposes. I hope I have made myself clear to my right hon. friend. The Justice department bears out my interpretation, and backs up their interpretation with the statement sent to my department when the bill was submitted to them that the bill stated exactly the intention of the act in the clearest kind of words.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Has the minister the
ruling of the Justice department in writing?

Gold and Silver Marking

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext:
If my right hon. friend doubts
the statement for one minute I will have no trouble in obtaining the opinion in writing. It was stated most emphatically. Sometimes it does not suit my right hon. friend to call for things in writing. I would remind him of an occasion when he debated the wording of an order in council for over an hour. He said that the wording was the most clumsy wording that could be produced, 4 p.m. and yet when it was produced it was found to be the baby of my right hon. friend.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext: What one was that?

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext: Ten yeaTS ago.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext: Can the minister identify it?

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will turn
up Hansard he can find it.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I have not had much
time to come to any practical conclusion. The only one that I have come to is that the minister is absolutely hopeless. He, comes to the House now and tells us that the Justice department confirmed every interpretation he gave when the subject was last under debate. Well, if he had produced the opinion of the Justice department and read it to the House, I am quite certain that all members of the House would have understood it.
As it is, I fancy that no human being understands what the Justice department's opinion is. If it is that which the minister has set forth;-well., I was going to say it is nonsense, but I will not say that, because I know the opinion of the Justice department is not that; I am quite certain it is not. I have no doubt at all that the Justice department declared the words to mean just what they say; and I do not think there is any difference of opinion in the House, as to what they mean. In fact, I do not think that there is any difference of opinion except in the minister's mind, and I am afraid he is still under a misapprehension. My conclusion, therefore, is that the minister is hopeless. The confusion on the last occasion was due to the minister's persistence in the view that the effect of this clause, just as it stands, was to compel all articles, in regard to which the word "platinum" or any compound thereof was used, to be 95 per cent platinum. No one, else took that view, not even the hon. member for Battleford (Mr. McComica) who was so sure about the matter.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext:
If my right hon. friend will
read Hansard of yesterday he will see that he himself thought it meant that.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext:
This minister is more
hopbless than ever; I never said that nor did anyone ever think it, except himself. The minister should first understand the Department of Justice and then repeat their opinion accurately to the House. He has not done that. What the Department of Justice told him, I have no doubt, was that the clause means precisely what it says; and what it says is that the platinum, or the substance purporting to be platinum, shall be 95 per cent element platinum or platinum with iridium.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext: That is not correct.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext: I think the minister had better get the opinion of the department and read it.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext: Read the section; it covers it.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext: We have all read it and we know what it means; the only one who is confused about it is the minister. Some of the rest of us thought that while there was no question as to the meaning of the clause it would be better if it were worded in the form used before, both because it would be clearer and because that form was the established one. But as to what the effect of this is, there was no difference of opinion in the House, and there is no difference of opinion among hon. members now. The minister seems utterly incapable of getting the meaning of the words. So far as I am concerned, as the minister seems hopeless, he may go ahead and pass the legislation in any shape he wants.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext: I asked the minister yesterday a question which he did not answer. Is this intended to apply to the whole article or only to the plate surface?

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext:
It is intended to apply to all
articles containing at least 95 per cent pure platinum. Is that not plain enough?

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext:
1 have the utmost respect for the minister and I do not believe he is trying to evade the question; but certainly he is not answering it. Let me put it to him again. We have a ring, say:	Is this clause
intended to mean that 95 per cent of the entire ring is to be platinum or iridium? Or, if that ring is plated with platinum, does it mean that 95 per cent of the plate shall be platinum or iridium? That is what I want to know.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Ninety-five per cent of the
ring must be platinum. Surely, when 400 jewellers in the Dominion have requested that this legislation be passed, and have
Gold and Silver Marking

stated over the long distance telephone today that it is what they want, we ought to assume that they know what they want better than does the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen).

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext:
The minister seems to have
great faith in the hon. member for Brome (Mr. MeMaster), so far as this matter is concerned. At the bottom of the first column on page 3397 of Hansard there appears an amendment which I proposed which would make the point absolutely clear. I closed my remarks, after proposing the amendment, with these words:
That amendment would make it apply to the whole article and not merely to the plating upon it.
Mr. MeMaster:	That clearly is not the intention.
Yet the minister suggests to the House today that there is absolutely no doubt as to what the section means. I ask him to read that comment of the hon. member for Brome, in whose opinion he seems to have so much confidence; that hon. member took a view directly opposite to the construction which the minister puts upon the section.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Surely not.
M(r. BOYS: Pardon me, he does. I do not see the sense of this controversy, because we understand now that the intention is that the section shall apply to the whole article. I would suggest, in passing, in place of the cumbersome phraseology 950/1000ths the minister simply use the words 95 per cent. If 95 per cent of the whole article must be platinum or iridium there should be no difficulty about stating that in plain words; surely to goodness the English language is capable of such a use. The minister is positive to-day, but yesterday he was not so sure of himself. He has only to read the answers he made to the questions I put to him, to come to that conclusion; he has only to refer to what the hon. member for Brome and the hon. member for Victoria and Carleton both stated, to be convinced that his position has been wrong. There is not a single member who has spoken on this question who has not taken an opposite view to the minister's. Why not put the thing right? The public should be protected. If you buy a ring and it is said to be platinum you ought to know what you are getting. Do not let any jeweller or storekeeper be in a position to deceive the public. I am glad to hear the minister definitely say that this does mean that 95 per cent of the whole article is to be platinum. The section, however, to put it mildly, is most doubtful, and legislation, to be useful, should leave no room for doubt. I do not mean to say for a moment

that what I offered yesterday was the last word on the subject, but I do think that if the minister will adopt my suggestion he will find that it will clarify the intention which he seeks to convey; it will make the section very much clearer than it now stands.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I have no wish to delay the bill or to embarrass the minister, my sole concern being to see that both parties to the sale and purchase of platinum articles shall be protected. I quite agree with the minister that the jeweller is completely protected under this bill, but I do not think that the people who purchase the goods will be similarly protected. I direct the attention of the minister to the wording of the section:
The word " platinum " or any contraction, abbreviation or colourable imitation thereof shall not be applied, either alone or in combination with any other word, to any article of merchandise composed wholly or in part of any metal-
And so on. There is the point I refer to:
The section provides that the article may be "wholly or in part" of this metal.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I had the opinion of the
Deputy Minister of Justice, the Assistant Deputy Minister of Justice, another member of the same branch and the Law Clerk of the House, and these men state positively that the section is clear. Am I to listen to one or two members opposite and take their advice as against the advice of eminent lawyers such as Mr. Newcombe?

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext:
We are not pitting our opinion against that of the Deputy Minister of Justice on any matter of law, but the interpretation of this section is a matter of common sense. I agree with the minister that it means what it says, but I do not think that the section means what the minister says it means. I think the words "or in part" should be eliminated so that the section would properly read:
The word " platinum " or any contraction, abbreviation or colourable imitation thereof shall not be applied, either alone or in combination with any other word, to any article of merchandise composed wholly of any metal. .	.	.
If this section passes as drafted, in my opinion a jeweller would be able to -make a ring plated with platinum-if that is possible [DOT]

and if 95 per cent of the plating was platinum, to stamp it with the word "platinum", and the public might buy the ring believing it was solid platinum. If you cut out the words, "or in part", to my mind there would be no doubt as to what was meant; as the section stands I think its meaning is very

Gold and Silver Marking
doubtful. I believe, with the Justice department, that this section means just what it says, but apparently they were not able to convince the minister that it does.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext: Surely we agree that the clause means that any a/rticle upon which the word "platinum" is stamped must contain at least 950/1000ths, or 95 per cent, of pure platinum.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Then why are these
three words, "or in part" inserted?

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext:
The article must be either of
pure platinum or of platinum to the extent of 95 per cent.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Then why these words: "to any article of merchandise composed wholly or in part of any metal unless 950/1000ths of component parts of the metal appearing or purporting to be platinum of which said article consists"?
Mr. MoCONICA:	Let ujs suppose the
article is a diamond ring set in platinum, then the platinum would be platinum and the diamond would be diamond, and the whole thing would be a ring and would comply with this definition. If it were a shot gun, the barrels would be platinum and the stock would be wood, and it would comply with this provision.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext: No.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext:
So far as it purports
to be platinum it must be 95 per cent pure.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext: That is all right.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext:
That is what it says;
that is what it means; and that is what it is intended to mean.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext:
If my bon. friend can
get that into the minister's head he will be doing well.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Following the line of
reasoning of the member for Battleford (Mr. McConica), if a bar of half-inch iron is plated with platinum, then it can be stamped "platinum", because the part which purports bo be platinum, the plating, will comply with this section. I think the illustration of the member for Battleford should convince the minister that the section does not mean whit he thinks it means.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Let me call the minister's attention to a common article of jewellery, a lady's bar pin or bracelet jewelled. The jewels are actually set in platinum, but on account of the expense of that metal the balance of the metallic portion of the pin
or bracelet is made up of what is called white gold, bearing the appearance of platinum. Could an article of that kind be stamped "platinum?"

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Not unless it contains 950/
lOOOths of pure platinum or platinum in conjunction with iridium.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Then what is the object
of the words, as the bon. member for Victoria and Carleton (Mr. Caldwell) points out, "or in part?" The "part" of the article would be the clasp holding the stones, and it might be stamped "platinum" if those words are allowed to remain.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext:
The clasp must contain 95
per cent pure platinum or platinum in conjunction with iridium before the word "platinum" is allowed to be stamped upon it.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext: Then why not strike out those words, "or in part?"

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext:
If these words were deleted
it would not be permissible for the article to contain 5 per cent of any other metal than platinum.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext:
That is what I say, you
should not stamp the bracelet or pin "platinum" when the body of it is composed of white gold.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Do you contend that it should
be 100 per cent pure?

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext:
No, I mean the whole
article should be platinum, not part of it platinum and part of it white gold. I think the words "or in part" are objectionable there.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext: Possibly this will make it clear to the minister.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext: It will not.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Suppose the section
were altered to read, "any article of merchandise composed wholly of any metal of which 95 per cent shall be platinum?" Surely the minister would not contend that, so worded, the section would mean that the article must be 100 per cent platinum. I think that is as clear as day-it is to me. If the section read, "to any article of merchandise composed wholly of platinum unless 95 per cent was platinum," I admit the minister would be right, t'he article would have to be 100 per cent pure. Worded as I suggest, the clause is short and plain.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I did not
take any part in the discussion yesterday, indeed I did not listen very closely to it,
Gold and Silver Marking

and therefore I approach the matter entirely unprejudiced. I have read the section to see wihat interpretation I would put upon it. This is my interpretation: That the clause refers to the metal of Which, we will say, a ring is composed, and is intended to mean that 95 per cent of the metal which goes into the ring shall either be platinum or platinum in conjunction with iridium.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext: That is right.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext:
That is the meaning I put
upon this clause. In other words, whatever metal it is composed of, 95 per cent pure platinum or platinum in conjunction with some other metal shall form part of the whole composition.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext: That is the interpretation which I have placed on the clause for the last twenty-four hours, but my right hon. friend (Mr. Meighen) says I am "hopeless."

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext: I was not too "hopeless" to be returned for my constituency where I have resided for the past thirty-five years. I think it ill becomes my right hon. friend to interject such objectionable remarks into the discussion of a very simple bill. The interpretation which I have put upon the clause is exactly the same as the interpretation of the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown).

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I admit, though the
minister objects to the words, that they only express my feelings. I have done my best to explain to the minister what this section means, but without success; and from what he says I think the Deputy Minister of Justice has made a similar effort, but evidently he did not succeed any better.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Cannot I make my right hon.
friend (Mr. Meighen) understand-

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext: I understand the section as thoroughly as I ever understood anything.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext: -that any metal offered for sale as platinum, no matter what its metallic contents, must contain at least 95 per cent platinum alone or in conjunction with iridium before the word "platinum" can be stamped upon it. My right hon. friend suggested a few minutes ago that we make it read 100 per cent.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext: I never said that.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I think he referred to some
percentage.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext:
No.
[Mr. Brown.)

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Gold is treated in the same
way; it must contain 921 per cent pure gold before it is allowed to be stamped as gold.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext: I think this bill is of sufficient importance for us to understand what it means; otherwise how can we expect the public to understand it? If I followed the minister correctly, he says that the purpose of this bill is that any article offered for sale and stamped "platinum" must contain 95 per cent platinum. Is that correct?

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext:
That is correct. I am glad
that there is at least one member behind my right hon. friend (Mr. Meighen) who understands the meaning of this clause.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext:
The minister did not
allow me to finish. If this bill is for the protection of the public, then I say it does not accomplish that object, and I am not concerned with what the Minister of Justice or any one else may say about it. The bill says:
Any article of merchandise composed wholly or in part of any metal unless 950/1000ths of component parts of the metal appearing or purporting to be platinum-
And so on. Under that provision an article in which a stone is set may be stamped platinum if 95 per cent of the small portion surrounding the stone is pure platinum; the remainder can be any metal Whatever. That is the only interpretation to be put upon it.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext: I am glad at least that the hon. member agrees that it means 95 per cent platinum. I am willing to accept the opinion of such eminent lawyers as Mr. New-oombe, Mr. Edwards, the assistant deputy minister and another lawyer in the Department of Justice, experts in drawing bills, who passed upon this drafting. They say that the clause is as clear as it is possible to make it, and I am going to stand by that opinion of the Justice department.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext:
What did my
horn, friend submit to the department?

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I had my deputy go over to
the Justice department with me, taking the file of correspondence between the Department of Justice and the Department of Trade and Commerce in connection with the preparation of the bill. I took Hansard with me, showed them some statements of hon. members, and asked them whether the clause was sufficiently clear to carry out the intent of the measure. They said that the clause

Gold and Silver Marking
clearly provided that the article must contain 95 per cent of pure platinum or element platinum, and that no other words could make it clearer.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext: Perhaps the minister will do me this justice. I have said quite a little on this bill yesterday and to-day as to what it means. The minister has been trying hard to score on me by some indefinite references to something nobody ever heard of. But he will score wonderfully on me now if he will take from Hansard any sentence I have uttered as to the meaning of this clause and bring to the House a statement from the depnty minister that I am wrong to the extent of a shadow.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I am satisfied that this
bill does not carry out the minister's intention ; it does not protect the legitimate jewellery trade but will permit improper and unlawful marking of goods as platinum which are not platinum. These words "wholly or in part" in the fourth line are the words .that are going to create the difficulty. I cannot do better than give the minister the illustration I gave him before. Take the case of a jewelled bar pin where the jewels are actually set in platinum which is 95 per cent pure. The remainder of the pin, however, is white gold, made to resemble platinum-a very much cheaper metal. That bar pin is "wholly or in part" platinum and can be stamped "platinum" under the bill.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Not unless it contains 95 per
cent platinum.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext:
The bill says that the
article may be "wholly or in part" platinum. Part of that article is pure platinum, complying with the bill, and if an article which is wholly or in part pure platinum dan be stamped platinum, someone is going to be misled. I think these words "wholly or in part" should be struck out.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext:
There seems to be some
misunderstanding between the minister and the Justice department. I suggest that this item be dropped. I do not see why the minister should prolong the session a full week discussing his estimates.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I beg to correct my hon. friend.
I am not prolonging the session. Hon. members opposite are doing it.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext: It seems he is endeavouring to prevent his estimates going through.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext:
We are discussing Bill
No. 176, not the estimates.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I suggest that the minister
answer the questions that are put. I have been sympathetic toward the minister. We have been censured for offering so much criticism from this side, yet the minister himself provokes that criticism and I do not propose to sit here and listen to this discussion without saying what I want to say about it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext: Shall clause 2 carry?

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext:
It should not carry at
all.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I think we
are all agreed as to what the intent of the committee is with regard to this proposed measure. But the question has arisen whether the measure definitely expresses what the sense of the committee is. The minister says the bill was designed to carry out the clear intent as understood by the committee and that in having the bill prepared he went through the ordinary course followed by every minister in the preparation of legislation. It goes to the Department of Justice, and through them to the officials of the House, who supervise the drawing up of the measure, and the minister comes to the House and says: This is the measure intended to carry out what is now the purpose of the committee. One can argue and define as to the various interpretations that might be put upon a complicated sentence of this kind, but I do think that in view of the discussion that has taken place the committee can very safely adopt the wording that has been arranged by the law officers and advisers whose duty it is to put into language the intention of the minister or the department seeking the drafting of the legislation.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext: I welcome the advent of my hon. friend (Mr. Macdonald) into this discussion, because I appreciate now that we shall be able to get at least some consideration of a legal proposition. The first thing I am going to ask him is whether in his view this act should be made effective?

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext: We are all agreed about that.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext: Very good. I have got that from my hon. friend, but I could not get it yesterday. Well, if this act is to be made effective, ought platinum to be brought within the application of the act?

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext:
The whole issue, as my hon. friend sees, is whether or not those to whom is entrusted the task of trans-
Gold and Silver Marking

lating into language the ideas intended to be put on the statute books, have actually done so. My hon. friend says no; the minister is advised to the contrary.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext: I asked the minister what he submitted to the department. He did not submit any legal questions with which he was confronted in connection with this bill. Now I hope the Minister of National Defence is not going to run away.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext: I have to go to the Redistribution committee.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext: Then I shall have to fall back upon my hon. friend. I am going to assume that the Minister of Trade and Commerce wants this to be an effective bill.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext: We are agreed on that.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext: Then how can he make it effective unless the limiting clause of the act, which deals with the matters to which the act applies, is amended for the purpose of including platinum? How on earth can it be done? The trouble with my hon. friend is this: He has got jurt one idea into his head, that was this section, and he got it there with a certain degree of heat.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext: Oh, no.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Oh yes; with
a certain degree of heat and with the determination to bull the thing through, right or wrong. He goes to the department just with that one thought in his head-because I am sure the Department of Justice are not insane;
I felt sure, if the matter was drawn to their attention, just what they would do, and I took particular pains to ask my hon. friend what he submitted to them. What he submitted to them was this correspondence with the jewellers, and this section, and he asked them what this section meant. Now the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) joined with me absolutely in pointing out the necessity of making other alterations in this bill, and I am going over it again because the minister evidently forgot all about it, and these were the very questions that ought to have gone to the Justice department.
I point out to the minister again that section 2 of the act respecting the manufacture, marking and sale of articles composed of gold or silver, and of gold plated and silver plated ware, is the interpretation clause. You have the interpretation which is given to articles of gold and silver, and most particularly of marks. My hon. friend, when he looks at the statute, will find in regard to marks that that important definition limits it to

marks having regard to "quality, quantity or weight of gold or of silver, or quality or kind of gold or silver plate." It does not cover platinum at all. The platinum sections, if they are to be made workable, would certainly be much helped if the interpretation clause were extended to cover platinum. Now that has nothing to do with this section as a section at all; it has to do with the scheme of the legislation as such. My hon. friend says that he wants to make this act an act which will be enforceable. Against whom is this act to be enforceable? The "dealer" means "any person who is a manufacturer of, or a seller of, or dealer in, whether by wholesale or retail, any of the articles to which this act applies". I point that out to my hon. friend, and also the very next section, which gives the list of articles to which this act shall apply. There is not a bit of good in adding at the end a little clause like this without adding platinum to the general administrative sections of the act. The section is perfectly clear:
This act applies to the following articles when made in Canada by, or sold in Canada by, or imported or otherwise brought into Canada by dealers, that is to say, "gold articles,' "silver articles,'' and "plated articles'' of gold or silver.
Surely my hon. friend must see that in order to have this legislation right, that clause providing for the application of the act should also be amended. Now take for example this section:
When an article is composed of mechanism, works or movements and of a case or cover containing the mechanism, works or movements, a mark applied to the article shall be deemed not to be, nor to be intended to be, applied to the mechanism, works or movements.
I suppose my hon. friend wants that applied to platinum, too?

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext:
No, they did not ask for
that.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Then, look at
the perfect ridiculousness of the situation we are getting into if that is not to be. If my hon. friend is right in that, a platinum watch cannot be stamped platinum, just like a gold or silver watch is stamped gold or silver, for the simple reason, according to my hon. friend, that the mechanism, works or movement it contains are not composed of platinum. Now, no sane man in the world thinks any one intends that.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext:
The word platinum is applied
in that case in much the same way as when you take a deed of a building, for instance, that includes all articles that are attached to the floor and walls. I do not think that it

Gold and Silver Marking
could be said that the works of a watch are a part of the case. If the works are taken into consideration the whole * watch may be very much under 925/1000t.hs parts of fineness, yet the act provides that you can stamp that watch "gold". Am I right?

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Yes, because
there is a provision for that. I asked my hon. friend if he wants a similar provision with regard to platinum, and he says no.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext: What is the provision protecting the watch?

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I have just
read it to my hon. friend. Now my hon. friend says that does not apply, that if you do not have a similar section with regard to platinum you can never stamp "platinum" on a platinum cover. But what my hon. friend says about gold is not quite right. You have a varying standard recognized for gold.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I understood a provision to be
read fixing a certain percentage in the case of gold.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext: The clause read out had reference to silver and not gold.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext: Well then, take the law in connection with silver.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Does my hon.
friend want the penal clause as to marks to apply here?

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext: Certainly they will apply.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Well, as the
bill is worded they do not apply. I again point out to 'the minister that he did not bring to the attention of the Department of Justice the very matters we are discussing upon Which the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) and myself are in absolute agreement.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I explained earlier in the day
that I had discussed this matter with the Department of Justice. I asked the department for an interpretation of the clause that was under discussion yesterday afternoon, as to whether the meaning of what was intended was plain and clear. The Department of Justice said they did not think it would be possible to make the meaning clearer than the words of the proposed amendment to the act made it. I asked the department what percentage of platinum should be contained in an article to which the name "platinum" might be applied. The department informed me that it was 95 per cent, that as the bill was drawn each article which had the word *"platinum" on it should contain at least
950/1000ths, which is 95 per cent. That is the interpretation I received from the Department of Justice together with the opinion that the meaning of the clause referred to could not be made plainer.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext: As to the plainness of the clause it is a matter of opinion. As to the meaning of the clause it is not a matter of opinion, it is very clear, I would not have risen but I see the Assistant Deputy Minister of Justice here, and I am going to put the two interpretations in his hearing and ask him to give the opinion of the department as to which it is. The question is this: Whether in the case of an article, a single article, as respects which part purports to be platinum and part not, this bill insists that the whole article shall be 95 per cent platinum or part platinum and part iridium, or whether only the part that purports to be platinum shall be 95 per cent platinum and iridum? I want the assistant deputy minister to answer himself.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext:
We heard him
answer. It confirms what we say ourselves.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext:
It was made clear by my
deputy and myself that it was 95 per cent of the whole article.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext:
That is not what the
assistant deputy minister said at all. I want the minister to answer right out.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I am always willing to admit
when I am wrong. I am not a lawyer and I accepted the interpretation that it was 95 per cent. My deputy was with me and that was the understanding he got also.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext:
The Assistant Deputy
Minister of Justice has just said to the minister that it was 95 per cent only of the part which purported to be platinum, not 95 per cent of the whole article. That is what the assistant deputy minister said; I heard him. That has been our whole contention. I tried to get it across to the minister for hours but I failed.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext:
In view of the presence of the Assistant Deputy Minister of Justice I would suggest that the words "wholly or in part" in the fourth line and the words "appearing or purporting to be platinum" in the sixth line be omitted, and I ask the assistant deputy minister whether this would not convey exactly what the minister wants? I am clear as to what the minister wants and I desire to see his wishes carried out, not to
Gold and Silver Marking

oppose the bill at all, but my contention is the present wording will not accomplish what he wants. If I were a jeweller I should like to see this provision passed into law just as it is.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I wish to say further that the
understanding I have mentioned was the understanding my deputy and myself gathered of the interpretation of the provision when we left the Department of Justice. Furthermore, my deputy called up the president of the Jewellers' Association, so that there might be no misunderstanding in the matter, and the president said the requirement was that it must be 95 per cent.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I know what the hon.
member for Victoria and Carleton (Mr. Caldwell) has in his mind and it is possible he is right. That is merely a matter of legislation. As to what the act means is not even a rhatter of opinion. There can be no possible two opinions on the subject; the opinion is just what the Assistant Deputy Minister of Justice told the minister a while ago, and what we have contended for for two days. I do not think it is the object of either the Jewellers' Association or the framer of the bill that the whole article should be 95 per cent platinum.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext: That is what he said.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I think the minister is
wrong as to that. I think the minister is wrong also as to what has been told him by the Department of Justice. Take a watch that may be studded with platinum-I am not very sure whether they are or not but they may be-it would never do to say that watch must be 95 per cent platinum or iridium but only the part Which purports to be platinum or as to Which any imitation of it is used. In so far as the existing section is concerned it means what the Justice department want it to mean, there is no doubt about that. The language used as respects silver and also gold could be clearer but its meaning is all right.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext:
The right hon. leader of the opposition would not propose to allow a jeweller to mark a watch "platinum" when it was only studded with platinum.
Mr. MEI'GHEN:	No. I do not know
whether platinum is used as a plating or not; but assuming it is, it would be quite lawful for the jeweller to stud, a ring with platinum plate providing it had ninety-five per cent platinum or iridium. It would be quite 
proper to stud a watch with platinum, provided the platinum in it was ninety-five per cent pure; but it would not be proper to call it a platinum watch.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext: He could under the act.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext: Under this act possibly he could; but under the law generally, without this section he could not, because it is not a platinum watch.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext: Then this would make illegal what is now legal?

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext: Under the present law if a man misrepresents anything he is liable for misrepresentation. He is not liable to the penalties of this act, but to the general penalty, and a jeweller who would say that a ring was platinum when it was only platinum plate would be liable for misrepresentation under the law. I think it is assuming a grave responsibility to make this mean what the hon. minister states.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext:
He might not state
that it was a platinum ring; but under the law he would be allowed to stamp "platinum" on it if it were ninety-five per cent platinum?

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext: No, this act merely says what he cannot do. It does not deny him the right to do what it defines, but the ordinary law of the land denies that right. This bill comes in and defines a new class of offence.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext: If the bill is not clear, I do not want to press it. I want to make sure.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext:
If my suggestion to
strike out certain words in the fourth and sixth lines were adopted, would it not make it clear that the article must be ninety-five per cent platinum?

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext: The deputy informs me that if the word "platinum" is applied to an article it must be ninety-five per cent platinum. If you. bought an article stamped "platinum" you would assume you were buying something which was ninety-five per cent platinum.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext: Any person who understands the primary principles of law knows that the contention of the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) is correct; but I think the wording of the bill is not very plain, and I would suggest that we waste no more time, but postpone the measure and endeavour to get together on it.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I think that would be the
best thing to do. The minister should try to bring the bill back in proper shape. It would take hours in committee to put it in proper form.

Gold and Silver Marking

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext: It seems to me that this bill means just what it is intended to mean, and that it will do just exactly what it is intended to do. It provides that a platinum article shall contain ninety-five per cent platinum. If it is composed partly of platinum and partly of some other material, the part that is platinum must be ninety-five per cent platinum.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext:
If the portion which is
required to be platinum is only ninety-five per cent platinum, why should the dealer call the whole thing platinum?

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext: That is our point.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext: The leader of the opposition is correct in his contention.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I am glad that
the hon. member for Hants (Mr. Martell) has come to our assistance, because perhaps we can postpone consideration of this measure for the present and deal with other matters. We should make this a workable bill. The only thing to do is to bring platinum within the interpretation clause, which is the second clause. Clause 3 specifically confines the application of the act to gold and silver. The word "platinum" should 'be inserted in the clause. If we are to go after platinum dealers, we must make it apply to those dealers.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext:
The deputy minister informs
me that if an article is made up of fifty per cent platinum and fifty per cent something else the word "platinum" could not be applied to it. If the word "platinum" were applied to it, it would have to be applied to a platinum tip or something of that kind. I merely say this to show that this morn-5 p.m. ing I honestly interpreted the remarks of the deputy minister, to mean that every article must contain ninety-five per cent of platinum.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I have never foi} a
moment disputed that the minister honestly sought to interpret what was given to him, but he did not comprehend what it meant, and when one tries earnestly to make a thing clear the minister should not hark back to other matters.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext: The right hon. member should not cast slurs on the department and refer to the minister as "hopeless."

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext:
There were no slurs at
all; but the minister comes back with something else and talks about divisions between lawyers and so on. The minister is not a lawyer. It is not necessary to be a lawyer
to understand this section. If the minister has spent his life in other lines and is not accustomed to this class of work, he should be a little more patient. I think this lesson to-day will teach him in future to be more patient, and not get into difficulties.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT 1913. AMENDMENT
speechtext:
The reason I relied on the
Justice department and the law clerk of the House was because I was not a lawyer and knew nothing about it. The Assistant Deputy Minister of Justice now tells me that when articles are composed of fifty per cent platinum and fifty per cent other material the word "platinum" could not be applied to the whole.
I ask that the section be allowed to stand.
Section stands.
Progress reported.

Hon. A. B. COPP (Secretary of State) moved the second reading of Bill No 118, to amend the Companies Act.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the House went into committee thereon Mr. Gordon in the chair.
On the short title.

I cannot remember the
minister ever having given an explanation in detail of the general purpose of the bill.

I have not made any general
statement inasmuch as the bill involves a good many minor amendments which are intended to correct certain anomalies in the act. The act has been amended from time to time and the language of the various amendments is not uniform; the majority of the amendments are intended to rectify that. There are six or seven new sections which can be studied as we proceed. The amending bill has been considered by the leading corporation lawyers in different parts of the Dominion in consultation with the law officers of the department and the amendments which are now suggested are the result of those conferences. Last year a good many similar amendments were passed in this House but they were dropped in the Senate owing to pressure there; I understand that they were omitted not because of any particular objections to them but wholly for the reason I have stated. In the hurry and rush they were scuttled so to speak. Since that time and during the present session very strong representations have been made by lawyers who frequently resort to the act, to have these amendments carried. The amendments are intricate but I am sure that legal gentlemen in the committee will be able to follow the explanatory notes.
Companies Act

What protection
is given the public in relation to what is commonly called watered stock? Is any definite provision made in that regard?

Provision is made in the act
itself with regard to watered stock but there is nothing in these amendments on that subject.

Is there adequate
protection in the act to safeguard the people against watered stock?
Yes, in the act itself.
What is it?
I cannot tell the hon. gentleman offhand just what the provisions are but he will find on page 13 of the act just how the matter of watered stock is provided for.

I am not a lawyer and am therefore unable to discuss the legal aspect of this bill. I think the House made a mistake in allowing the bill to go into committee without some consideration of the general principles involved. The -bill was moved into committee before I had an opportunity of looking it up and I submit that we should have some explanation on the part of the minister of its general principles. Here a question has come up with regard to the issuing of watered stock; the minister should explain the principal features of the bill including this matter.

Section agreed to.
On section 2-When company may be created a private company.

What is the
distinction between a private company and a general company?

This amendment is simply to
conform with subsection 3 of section 43 of the act.
I have not the act here.

Subsection 3 of section 43
refers to private companies but there is no provision for the creation of private companies. This section provides the necessary machinery for constituting such companies.
I understand that, but what is the real distinction, for the purpose of the act, between a private and an ordinary company.
The difference consists in the limitation of shares to the public in the case of the private company.

I have not had much to do with companies of that sort but I should think that a private company would differ from an ordinary company only in this, that whereas in the case of the general company the stock may be sold to the public generally, the stock in a private company is restricted to a number of shareholders, and there may be certain restrictions in the method of transfer. I am not attempting to explain the distinction, but that is the only difference that I can see.

The hon. member's explanation would seem to be right. But what is the public policy that suggests the necessity for a private company? What is the object of this legislation and what is to be gained by it?
Mr. COPP; I am instructed that it applies to a company whose stock is not offered to the public but is held by, say, the members of a family-a private company. That is one illustration.

That can be done today under the Canada Companies Act. As a general rule a certain number of persons, three in Nova Scotia, five in the other provinces, can secure incorporation and their powers are set forth in the memorandum of association which they file, which powers must be in consonance with what the general act authorizes. Supposing these people get a charter for a company with a capitalization of $50,000, in one dollar shares, there is nothing to prevent them from owning those shares.

In the case of
insurance companies we have a superintendent of insurance w'ho insists upon certain requirements -being complied with before a company can be organized. Is there any similar scrutiny exercised an regard to the formation o-f such a company as this?
The applicants for the incorporation of a company must comply with the provisions of the Companies Act.

Is there any
scrutiny by the minister's department of any of the statements made by the promoters?

The promoters -must file their
prospectus with the Department of the Secretary of State.
Then you take the statements in the prospectus at their face value?

The department do not scrutinize the prospectus particularly, but those

Companies Act
who are considering the advisability of buying stock may come to the department and study the prospectus. They must use their own judgment in regard to its contents.

This does not apply to
insurance companies, but only to ordinary trading companies.
Yes.

My thought was
not that insurance entered into this, but I said that in the case of insurance companies the public has some guarantee of their soundness. Is there any similar guarantee in the case of these companies?

These private
companies are prohibited from inviting the public to subscribe for any debentures or shares. This section applies to a limited partnership form of company, and I do not see any objection to it.

While the prohibition
applies to invitations to the public to subscribe for debentures or shares, does it prevent a, shareholder from selling his stock to the public?
He can sell stock, but only to a limited extent.

You are putting in a
prohibition so the incorporators can keep the stock within their own narrow bounds. But the law to-day would allow it to be done by agreement among the shareholders themselves.

Section agreed to.
On section 3-Applicants.
Is there any provision that the provisional directors shall hold office for any particular length of time, or that they have any real interest in the concern?

Under the provisions of the
Companies Act provisional directors are appointed until such time as the company is organized and the shareholders elect their directors. This amendment makes no change.

Section agreed to.
On section 4-Applicants.
This section appears to me to be intended to make it clear that the provisions apply only to companies without share capital; is that it?

Yes.
!
They were intended to apply only to companies with share capital. If that be the case, it is to get rid of the possibility of error?
Yes.
There are a lot of subsections. What is the idea in subsection (6)? It is pretty hard to follow that.
It is to correct a clerical error. In the old act it appears as subsection 2; it should be subsection 3. That is the only change.

Section agreed to.
'On section 5-subsection (1)-Issue of shares without nominal or par value.-Statement as to preferred stock.

What does the
minister say about this?

The note gives an explanation of the amendment. It refers to the formation of a company issuing stock without par value. A similar provision has been in force in the United States and in the province of Ontario lor a number of years, and corporation lawyers inform me that it is working very satisfactorily. We are simply bringing our act into uniformity with it.

Is there a similar clause
in the English Companies Act?

Our original
legislation, if I recollect aright, was based on legislation of the state of New York so far as this no money share amendment is concerned.
It was adopted in 1897.

I do not think
England had covered it in their General Companies Act.
No.

I understand
that all that is being done here is to ingraft on the American statute: we took over the amendments which the Americans have found it necessary to make.
That is right.

Subsection agreed to.
On subsection (2)-Equality of shares.
That is in the same position I assume?
Yes.

Subsection agreed to.
Companies Act
On subsection (3)-Shares to be allotted at price fixed by board or letters patent.
In paying a dividend would these shares without par value be entitled to participation the same as shares with par value?
They might declare a dividend on the value of the shares.

But they are without
par value.
They do not pay any percentage dividend on the shares but if the company make sufficient to pay dividends they may pay at the rate of so much per share.

I would like to get
that clear. Do these shares have the same right to dividend as shares in the same company that have a par value?

It. depends on whether the
company p:e making enough money to pay the dividend.

Under this act we are
allowing the company to issue non par value shares. Does that mean shares of stock for which no money is paid?

No. We issue a charter to the company for no capital stock but for a certain number of shares and the directors fix the values of the shares and sell them accordingly. That value may also be fixed by the charter.

The only difference between this arrangement and the provision under which when a company is incorporated it has so many thousand shares of stock is that the shares here have no money value. Theoretically the entity is split up into say a thousand different shares and the owner of each share is entitled to one-thousandth part as an owner of that property. In the other case he is entitled to a share which represents so much in money value. That value is supposed to be properly related to the value of the property it represents though that of course is not always the case. In this instance there could be a multiple of shares; there is no question about that. But these shares with no money value represent nothing but an individual interest in the assets of the company. The company is incorporated, and at the incorporation the price at which the shares shall be disposed of may be arranged. On the other hand-
I speak now subject to qualification-the directors may by by-law say at what price the shares shall be sold. Obviously therefore, when you get to that point you cannot declare

a definite dividend of a certain per cent because there is no definition of money value in the hands of the shareholders on which the dividend may be computed. So what is done is this; the directors define what shall represent the amount available for the distribution of profits, and as soon as the amount so available is declared each one of these shares of no money value is entitled to an amount proportionate to the relation which it bears to other shares outstanding.

That is quite clear. A company gets a charter to do business. There is no capital stock, but they have say a thousand shares of no money value. Does this mean that the company may issue only a thousand shares? Because if] jthey, could continue issuing their shares it would mean that the shareholders would not be entitled to the one-thousandth part.

They may issue only the
thousand.

Then the earnings of
the company are divided pro rata among the thousand shareholders, or if a loss is made it is borne proportionately fey those shareholders?
Yes.

I think there are some members who would like to know from the minister what steps are taken to protect the public so far as the sale of shares is concerned. I think this is the matter which has been referred to by the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth). I am now referring particularly to the various types of provincial legislation. In some of our provinces we have what is sometimes denominated as "blue sky legislation," providing certain safeguards to the public in the event of the sale of shares by corporations. What provision is made by the Dominion under the Companies Act for the protection of the public in a similar manner?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The discussion must be strictly relevant to the clause under consideration. This matter could be considered under section 14.
Mr. SHAW':	Or section 8.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Section 8 covers only
commissions.

It goes further and deals with
shares offered to the public.

Section agreed to.	.

Companies Act
On section 6-Company may obtain change of name.

What does this
involve?

The wording of several sections of the act pi-oviding that certain transactions may be effected by a tworthirds vote is not uniform, and doubt has arisen whether "two-thirds vote" means two-thirds of all the issued capital or two-thirds of those present at the meeting of shareholders. The only change made here is that there must be a two-thirds vote of the shareholders present.

Present and
voting.
Yes.

Section agreed to.
On section 7-When company may surrender charter.

I suppose this
is to make it more certain that the shareholders' rights are considered.

It is the same provision we
have had for fifty years. A company may get a charter and may never organize, and the practice now is that they may return their charter to the department. This is to provide that they may return the charter under the act, provide the debts and everything of that nature are taken care of.
I do not see anything about insolvency here. What happens in that case?

They cannot surrender their
charter if they are insolvent.

But suppose a
company goes out of business entirely as a result of insolvency, what happens? Has the Secretary of State still to send out notices and get them back again like he did before?

They would be wound up in
the regular way.

They might or
might not. I thought the idea of this was to save the department sending out forms.

That is true, but the charter
can only be returned after the debts are all paid.

They have to comply
with all these terms before they can be liquidated.

If a firm goes through
the bankruptcy court, what becomes of their charter?

The order puts it out of
business.
Automatically?

Yes, but we are dealing here
with the case of a company being wound up.

When a charter is
surrendered, must it be with the unanimous consent of all the shareholders in the company? While the deputy is looking that up, I would like to give my reason for asking that question. We realize, of course, that in an incorporated company an agreement made by any authorized member of the firm binds every member of the firm, and that brings about the necessity of having the charter surrendered when they cease to do business as an aggregation. Take a hypothetical case. Suppose a company of three men is incorporated.

My hon. friend is not
quite correct. An incorporation is not a firm, and the shareholders of the company are not bound unless the agreement is within the four corners of the memorandum of association.

But until the charter is surrendered they are still a company in the eyes of the law, and any business contracted by any member of the firm is binding on the firm. Suppose there is a firm of three members and two of them wish the charter dissolved or surrendered, and the third objects. What is the procedure?

If they cannot come to
terms they would apply to the court, and the court would give some guarantee as to the rights of the minority in order that the company might be wound up, if the petition was for winding it up.
I presume that is correct, but I would like to have the minister's opinion.
If there was any such dispute there could not be a surrender of the charter, not unless everything was agreed upon and closed up by the shareholders, and the debts all paid.

Then it must be by
unanimous consent?
Yes.

Just what procedure
would you follow in the case I cited, where two members wanted to surrender the charter, and the third did not?

Companies Act

If anything was done, it
would have to be done by departmental regulation. There is nothing in this section providing for it.
Section agreed to.

Since the bill was drafted a
suggestion has come to us that we should add a new section, to be known as section 8, incorporating the provisions of the Companies' Act of Ontario. At the present time, a company when applying for a charter has to put in a long list of the objects of the company. This entails a great deal of work and expense in preparing the petition and sending it forward. This might be an appropriate time in view of the fact that we are discussing the protection of the public under this section, to draw the attention of the minister and hon. members generally to the situation with regard to the sale of shares so far as Dominion corporations are concerned. Everybody is familiar with the regulatory legislation passed by some four or five legislatures in Canada providing restrictions in connection with the sale of shares. May I be permitted to refer to the nature of that legislation. We have, for example, what is called the Sale of Shares Act in the province of Alberta passed in April 1916. Under this a company which proposes to sell its shares to the public must make application to the Board of Public Utility Commissioners, and these are some of the requirements which must be satisfied before the necessary certificate is given:
A company applying for permission to sell shares must satisfy the board as to the bona fides of the enterprise; that the company has a reasonable chance of success; and that the subscribers will have a fair run for their money.
In the case of a mining company the board requires a report by a competent engineer or, if a mere prospect, possibly a report by a geologist. The board may also require a report by an engineer or geologist of its own selection.
Promoters are frequently required to put up substantial financial assistance themselves. Promoters or vendors' stock must be put in escrow until the company proves its claim. Extravagant commissions are not allowed.
The minimum subscription upon which a company proceeds to allotment must be a substantial one. Experience has shown that many companies never obtain anything like sufficient to begin operations, and upon winding-up proceedings the proceeds of the stock subscribed are eaten up in costs, commissions, and other expenses.
Now, similar legislation has been enacted, in various provinces of Canada including the province of Ontario, where the legislation became effective some short time ago. So far as the Dominion is concerned there is no provision in the Federal Companies Act which is at all comparable with the legislation which I have indicated. The promoters of a company

Companies Act
need only seek incorporation, and then they have the right to sell their shares practically without any limitation. There are some minor limitations, but, as I suggest, nothing which at all compares with the restrictions imposed by the provincial acts. The next thing is that some of these provincial legislatures have sought to make the legislation they have passed applicable to Dominion companies. That was tried in the province of Saskatchewan where a case of this character arose: A company validly incorporated under this very act, amendments to which we are now considering, sold some of its shares to a resident of Saskatchewan. He was not able to pay in full so he gave a promissory note for the balance remaining unpaid. He did not pay the promissory note when it fell due, and the Dominion corporation consequently sued him. He defended the action on the ground that the Dominion corporation had not prior to the sale of the shares secured the necessary certificate from the local government board in Saskatchewan. The company replied that the Sale of Shares Act of Saskatchewan was ultra vires of the province so far as it attempted to interfere 'with the Dominion corporation. It was urged that the right to sell shares is an inherent right in a corporation, and consequently a corporation validly incorporated under the Dominion Companies Act has the inherent right to sell its shares without any restriction by provincial legislation. The case went to the Appeal court of Saskatchewan, and that court unanimously held that the Sale of Shares Act of Saskatchewan, so far as it purported to affect the selling of shares by a Dominion corporation, was absolutely invalid. The case was appealed to the Supreme Court of Canada, and judgment was given some months ago affirming the decision of the Appeal Court of Saskatchewan.
What was the case?

The case before the Saskatchewan court was the Ruthenian Farmers Elevator Company vs. Lukey, with the Attorney General of Saskatchewan intervening, and the report will be found in volume 3 of the Weekly Western Law Reports (1923) at page 138. That is the situation, and the result is that when a company which is formed for a speculative enterprise or a questionable purpose, is unable, under the existing provincial legislation in some provinces, to sell its shares, all it needs to do is to come down to the Dominion government and seek incorporation; then it is permitted without restraint of any kind to sell its shares in any part of Canada. I think that is a highly undesirable state of affairs. Not only does it permit these speculative companies to so sell
their shares to the public, but, in addition to that, it largely nullifies the provincial legislation; because of course when such legislation is passed by the provincial government it becomes absolutely ineffective, for the reason that these companies immediately seek Dominion incorporation. I regret that the minister has not taken some steps to meet that situation and to provide some sort of organization or some regulation which will be comparable in its nature to the legislation I have indicated, and which is now in force in, I think, at least six provinces of the Dominion. I bring it to the attention of the minister because it is a matter of vital importance. It is important that in this respect the interests of the public should be protected. Some other hon. gentlemen are interested, I believe, in presenting some other phases of the matter for the consideration of the minister, but I bring to his consideration primarily the legal situation that exists; so that he may if he deems it advisable, take the necessaiy steps to provide a remedy, either by incorporating the necessary legislation in the Dominion Companies Act, or perhaps by giving power to the provincial governments to control the sale of shares by Dominion corporations.

This very same question
has recently been the subject of a judicial decision in the province of New Brunswick, and arose directly under the provincial legislation in that province providing for the issue of certificates by the Public Utilities Commission before stock could be legitimately sold. The promoter of the company was fined in the police court in St. John, and the conviction was taken up, by way of certiorari, to the Court of Appeal and quashed on the very ground stated by the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Shaw). That is now the law of the province of New Brunswick, and the provincial act is practically rendered worthless. The provincial legislation which sought, as everybody is aware, to control the sale of wildcat shares, has been thereby rendered more or less of a dead letter, because corporations of this character immediately become incorporated under a Dominion charter and place the provincial laws at defiance. I think the time is opportune to have an expression of opinion as to the policy of the government on this so-called blue sky legislation, and I would invite the minister to make a statement to the House and the country on this point.

This matter has been under
consideration, and is being considered now by the departmental officials, and I have a very long and voluminous opinion here con-
Companies Act

taming some fifteen pages in regard to the matter; but we thought the investigation had not been carried sufficiently far to come to a conclusion as to whether or not legislation should be brought down at the moment. We have my hon. friend's statement that a conviction1 made under the act has been quashed by the Appeal court which renders the provincial law practically a dead letter. I would not like to say to the committee just what legislation should be brought down with regard to it, but the officers and legal officials of the department have given a great deal of thought to the matter. That is to say, the minister and his department have not any opinion on the subject. That is about what his statement amounts to. This matter has been before the public for quite a number of years, as stated by the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Shaw). In New Brunswick the act is on the statute book and may be brought into effect by proclamation.

government not pass an act called An Act respecting the Sale of Securities?

My hon. friend may be
right. My recollection was that the so-called blue sky law of Ontario was the product of the brain of ex-Attorney General Raney, of unhappy memory, and that it had never been proclaimed.

Ontario legislature, and is called The Sale of Securities Act, 1924.

My information is that
it was not passed, but I speak subject to correction. I think it is of sufficient importance to have an expression of opinion from the department, if it has an opinion. If the minister is not prepared to go any further than to say that the department is studying the question, we wall have, to be content with that for the present, but the matter is of very great importance, and I know that there are two schools of thought in connection with the matter. I have not much sympathy with a lot of paternal legislation that is on the statute books at the moment. I think we have altogether too much of it, At the same time there is a great deal to be said in favour of such legislation.

It seems to me this is a
matter of very great importance, and I should like some declaration from the minister as to his intentions next year, if not this year.
He says that 'his department is
9 p.m. studying the matter. Well, I can quite understand the desirability of considering the details, but surely it wo-uld be easy enough to make some statement as to the general intention, as to whether or not they consider legislation in this direction desirable. Surely the House is entitled to some declaration in this matter; and I hope the declaration will be favourable, because it is a scandalous thing that companies should be able to evade the intention and effect of provincial legislation by incorporating under Dominion charters. I hope the minister can give the House some assurance that this matter will be dealt with in the right way at the earliest possible date.

I can assure my hon. friend
that, so far as the department is concerned, when the matter is dealt with it will be dealt with in the right way, if the right way can be found.
