The department is in communication with the attorneys general of the different provinces and we shall be delighted to co-operate in every way possible with a view to devising some legislation that will be satisfactory both

Companies Act
to the provinces and to hhie Dominion,. The matter has been more particularly brought to the attention of the department by reason of the recent cases to Which 'hon. gentlemen have referred. The law officers are giving the subject their best consideration, and I trust that before long we shall see our way clear to introduce legislation, that will fully meet the situation, providing protection to all parties concerned, both the companies and prospective shareholders. As my hon. friend (Mr. Hanson) has rightly said, there are two schools of thought, and the matter is of sufficient importance to call for the utmost consideration.

To which school of thought
does the minister adhere?

I am not expressing a personal
opinion.

I gather from the
minister that this section is copied from the British act; and there is a similar section in the statutes of Ontario relating to companies. There is also a section very much to the same effect in the Companies Act of Nova Scotia. I agree with the hon. gentleman (Mr. Hanson) that there are two schools of thought, and he says that he has very little sympathy with much of paternalistic legislation. The hon. gentleman and I cannot always concur on matters of political dogma, but when it comes to a question of this kind I am heart and soul with him. I do not believe that there is any country whose laws are better fitted, as a model after which we can frame our own so that they may be acceptable to our people, than are the laws of England. We in the province olf Nova ISteotia 'claim that our general laws have been moulded on those of the Old Country; and after that, if we have no particular law of our own regarding some special matter, we sometimes seek advice from Ontario. But we do not always do that; my hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Hocken) and I would not always agree in that respdct. In the interpretation of statutes it is well to have precedents to guide us and if we have this section drafted after the British and Ontario sections, should a case come up under it we can consult our precedents as found in English and Ontario decisions. So that we will have a continuous system of law coming down to us. But if we are going to follow those people whose heads are up in the clouds and who are constantly looking for something to reform we shall never have any stability in the jurisprudence of the country. It is all very well to say that we should have blue
sky laws; but does not the act itself go as far as men should go? Are we not going to leave something to the intelligence of the people? We do not want parliament or the government to be a sort of godfather or godmother to every citizen in the country; we should give some of the people at least credit for having a little common sense and business acumen. And this very often is not displayed by a great number of those people who want legislation to meet every possible phase of any question that might arise. They seem to be afraid of the lawyers; but I notice that when matters come up in the House of Commons the lawyers have very little to say from the legal standpoint; we usually find lay lawyers giving advice on these points. My hon. friend from Victoria and Carleton (Mr. Caldwell) laughs, but there is no man who is as much a self-constituted philosopher and legal luminary as is the hon. gentleman, who speaks on everything under God's heaven. I am a humble member of the bar of Nova Scotia and I am going to say that the barristers of that province can hold their own with the lawyers of any other part of the country. I should have very little conceit in the ability of my fellow practitioners from that province if I did not say that. I am sick and tired of hearing people dictating to us on questions of legal interpretation and trying to tell the House what the law of the country on this and that subject ought to be, when they know absolutely nothing about it.
There are laws for the incorporation of companies in this country and there are divers kinds of corporations or incorporations. My hon. friend from South Simcoe (Mr. Boys) could tell us the nature of ecclesiastical corporations because I understand he is the chancellor of the Anglican diocese of Algoma.

I should be delighted to accept that compliment if I were entitled to it, but I do not want the House to have the impression which my hon. friend conveys. The hon. gentleman is thinking of a former member of the House, Mr. A. C. Boyce, then representing Algoma, and now on the Board of Railway Commissioners.

Well, I know there are various corporations and I thought that probably the hon. gentleman could tell us what ecclesiastical corporations were. There are different ways in which corporations can be brought in esse in this country; you can constitute them by act of parliament or by royal charter, and you can also have an incorporation under the Companies Act. The latter
Companies Act

is usually brought about by what is termed a memorandum of association, which sets out what are to be the powers of the company; and there are also articles of association setting out rules for the internal government of the company. Under this bill we are declaring what shall be set out in the memorandum of association and in the so-called prospectus; certain clauses are to state what the commission for selling shares shall be and what the prospectus shall disclose. But apart from what may be put into a statute regarding the prospectus there is also the common law. Every lawyer in the House is familiar with the case of Derry vs Peek. Under the common law, if' a man makes a fraudulent representation in the prospectus as to a matter of fact and is guilty of deceit or fraud there is a common law action against him in consequence. There is also action against the directors of a company if they do not act intra vires of the memorandum or charter of the company. These things are only fair. In this case the company in a certain prospectus offers shares and the people know what the prospectus states and what the memorandum of association contains; thus they know the powers of the company. If people are selling shares by making statements contrary to the authorized prospectus or are guilty of fraudulent representations of fact, they are liable under this bill; and there also lies action under the common law.
Surely in the name of everything that is fair we should leave something to the individual who wants to invest. Do not come here and circumscribe business with so many restrictions that people will not be inclined to invest at all. A good many members in this House seem to think that after they have taken the so-called gambler's chance the country should prosecute company promotel's simply because these gentlemen who invested of their own volition did not exercise good business ability. For heaven's sake do not surround business with too many restrictions. It is only fair that men should have complete freedom in their business transactions so long as they do not break the criminal law or infringe upon the common or statutory law rights of others. I claim that my hon. friend in introducing these amendments has adopted the principles of the British Companies Act, which are also to be found in the Ontario Companies Act-and Ontario is only second to Nova Scotia in matters of jurisprudence; you all know that and surely we as legislators should be prepared to follow British precedents, because we acknowledge that Great Britain has the fairest and most, equitable administration of 
justice of any country in the world, that there justice is always swift and impartial to poor as well as to rich. This being so, why should we, because owing to what I might describe as the fruits of the overheated brains of some people in this country, a new system has arisen-why should we, I say, think that we have a God-given right to disrupt the whole system of British jurisprudence on which our laws are founded? If we follow what has been been found to be sufficiently good in England in matters of law administration, I am quite confident that the people of this country will be well satisfied, because they will then know that their rights are protected and left equitably inviolate and that rich and poor alike, will enjoy liberty, equality and justice.

Mr. Chairman, I congratulate the hon. member for Hants (Mr. Martell) on his very able speech on the subject of the incorporation of companies, whether under provincial or federal jurisdiction. This is a matter of very grave concern to the business interests of the Dominion and to the people in general, and I sympathize very much with the minister in his desire not to express a very definite opinion on this very important question either in his own behalf or in the behalf of the government. We must realize that the parliament of Canada has inherent jurisdiction over the incorporation of companies, and I trust the day will never come when this" parliament will surrender that jurisdiction to any province; on the contrary, I hope that at all times it will conserve that right which was given to it when the constitutional act was passed for the confederation of the Dominion. Were we to follow the suggestion of my hon. friend from West Calgary (Mr. Shaw) and adopt the varying views of the provinces, we would sap that federal jurisdiction to its very foundation.

Does my hon. friend imagine that I suggested that the right of incorporation which e'xists in the Dominion government by reason of the Act of Confederation should be handed over entirely to the provinces?

No, I do not think my
hon. friend suggested that; but, as I understood him, his suggestion was that the right which we have should be circumscribed to fit in with the desires of the various provincial legislatures, and I think I am right in saying that in no two instances have the provinces passed the same legislation in regard to what is known as their blue sky laws. It is an accepted doctrine that, within their sphere the

Companies Act
provincial legislatures have the right to incorporate companies, and it is well known that they have gone beyond their powers in that respect; but so far as they have acted within their powers no objection can be taken. When, however, they seek to affect jurisdiction here to meet conditions in their own provinces and not generally applicable throughout Canada, then I submit they do seek to limit the jurisdiction and the authority of this parliament. I was under the impression that the Ontario legislature, while it had passed a blue sky law, had never yet brought it into force. My hon. friend from West Calgary mentioned that a law in respect of the sale of securities was passed by that legislature last session. I was not aware of it, although I remember seeing something in the newspapers that a bill for the purpose was introduced. But I accept my hon. friend's statement.

Might I say to my hon. friend, because I do not want to have any misapprehension on the point, that I observe in this particular act, which I am informed was passed lay the Ontario legislature last session, that it is to come into force on a date to be named by proclamation of the Lieutenant Governor in Council. So it may be as the hon. member suggests, not yet in effect.

Yes, perhaps it has not
yet been proclaimed. But the point I desire to impress on the minister is that this is a jurisdiction in respect of the incorporation of companies which this parliament must maintain; it is our duty to do so. We are not to be influenced by the whims of any government in any province. We must at all times be in a position to legislate for the benefit of the whole Dominion in matters which the British North America Act recognizes to be for the general advantage of Canada. That is an inherent duty on the part of this parliament, and I trust no government will ever surrender the right. New Brunswick has a law respecting the sale of securities in that province; another law exists in Saskatchewan; another in Alberta; another, I think, in Manitoba. Are we to be asked to frame a measure under our Dominion jurisdiction to meet all the requirements of these various provincial laws? Why the question has only to be stated to be denied. I submit it is not practicable, and I think if the government and the minister and the deputy minister,-whose familiarity with this question is far greater than that of any member in this House-if they devote themselves to framing a law which will be applicable to the whole Dominion on broad general principles such as we have always enjoyed, with
such reasonable safeguards as may be properly employed, then that is the extreme length to which this parliament should go in matters pertaining to the incorporation of companies.
I do not know that I have any very strong opinion with regard to paternalism, although I do believe that at the present time we are going to the very limit in that respect. But whether it is paternalism or not I do think there is wisdom shown in that which is offered to the public by the requirements of the proposed bill.

The hon. member
(Mr. Martell) is very much afraid of the result of overheated imagination, but it is rather strange that down in Nova Scotia they have actually passed blue sky legislation, also in New Brunswick, Quebec-

Tell us what the Nova
Scotia Act is and its effect.

-Ontario, Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta. Whatever may be the details of the acts in these provinces or however much they may differ, evidently the people there recognize the necessity of guarding the interests of the public. I take it that the hon. member (Mr. Shaw) was not urging that this Dominion should adopt exactly the clauses of these provincial acts but rather we should recognize that as the needs of the case have driven the provinces to legislate along this line, so the same needs should lead us to take action adequately to safeguard the interests of the people. I do not intend to speak with regard to the protection of the public from wildcat legislation, although I could instance some cases in my own province of Manitoba where I think many people are glad that they were saved from some schemes that were advanced a few years ago. I think particularly of one that was brought down from the city of Calgary, the home of my hon. friend (Mr. Shaw). Another very important problem closely related to this matter is the protection of the public from the mergers that are taking place, in the course of which the companies are being greatly over-capitalized. In the Farmer's Sun of October 15, 1921, there was published a study of some of the mergers that had taken place a few years ago, chiefly from 1905 to 1912, the period during which we had a very large number of consolidations in Canada. Already there has been put in equal quantities of "watered" stock and actual capital, and authority is given the companies to issue twice as much watered stock as actual money paid in. This is one of the most fruitful causes of the high cost of living. Every manufactured article is more or less affected by these mergers and the stock watering.
The public in my section of the country, whatever may be true of other parts of Canada, have awakened to the evils arising from this kind of thing. In the Grain Growers' Guide of November 16, 1921, there was a study based upon some articles that had appeared in the Monetary Times, which must be familiar to many in this House, showing the mergers which have taken place in the case of a number of leading corporations. I think it is recognized by all that undoubtedly over-capitalization increases the cost of commodities. The companies are of course, anxious to make their dividends on these high figures, figures that have no relationship to the amount of capital really put into the concern. I would like to point out also a hardship that is frequently worked upon the industrial population. Not only do the workers, as consumers, carry a heavy load in the enhanced cost of commodities, but they also frequently carry an additional burden in decreased wages. Many of these companies state they cannot afford to pay higher wages 
,and at the same time pay dividends. The following figures are interesting in this connection. They are taken from the Labour Gazette for May, 1924, pages 404 to 406:

It is not my intention, Mr. Chairman, to detain the committee with pointing the moral contained in these figures. I think we all recognize that the public ought to be safeguarded in some way against what might properly be called, irresponsible companies, companies that are not in any sense under existing regulations directly responsible to the people. These companies have very considerable power in their hands. They may make representations to the department, and so far as I can gather these representations are taken at their face value. There is no way, apparently in which the general public may be protected from-what shall I say?-the extortions of these companies. I think the member for Hants stated that we ought to be protected merely from deceit or fraud. I do not claim that from the strictly legal standpoint as the law now is on the statute books these companies are always guilty of deceit or fraud, but I do urge that if we consider the question from a higher aspect, we must admit that the companies have no moral right to charge prices for commodities that are not based on actual capital .invested. We must realize that people all over this country are recognizing that there must be a change. We are told, and my friends in the Farmers' group are told, again and again that the cost of living is high on account of the high wages. I submit that high wages are only one factor, and not the most important factor, in the cost of living to-day.

Are you sure your
professor is right?

I am quoting these figures from the Labour Gazette, not from the professor. Now let me impress upon the House this conclusion that we come to after studying these figures. We are returning to labour only 20 per cent of its average production. The percentage varies slightly in different countries; in the United States it is somewhat higher than in Canada at the moment. But, and this is my point, as long as you return to the producer of values only 20 per cent of those values how can they have consumptive power? The result must be stagnation. These things must be taken into account.
In conclusion let me submit, it is advisable that this government, and the minister particularly concerned, should take steps to stop this over-capitalization, and to protect the public from wildcat schemes. I would submit that a sworn statement should be demanded from incorporated companies showing the actual value of all tangible assets, and also an estimate of the value of all intangible assets, this sworn statement to be signed by an auditor. That would give the public some protection. We might then prohibit the giving of common stock as a bonus to the purchasers of bonds or preferred stock. I cannot for my life understand what justification there is for permitting companies to issue bonuses to those who will buy bonds or preferred stock. It looks very much like the giving of a prize, or something of that nature, with every pound of tea. Again why not insist that all common stock be sold at par and be fully paid up. I think that if these ideas were carried out they would form exceedingly valuable additions to the present legislation. An exception might be made in the case of highly speculative development industries such as mining, because enterprises of this character are required in the development of the country. But even in these cases supervision should be exercised by the department, and there should be a close examination undertaken by government officials before they were given the right to sell stock below par under any conditions. In the issue of the Monetary Times from which I have already quoted there are certain further recommendations which I desire to place on record.
1.	More information than hitherto afforded as to the past history and actual earnings of companies absorbed, must be given in the prospectus.
2.	The investor must know what was paid for the properties acquired by the consolidated company, and whether the consideration was cash, stock, bonds, or all three.

3.	Greater discretion and conservatism must be used in estimating the economies likely to accrue from amalgamation.
4.	Capitalization must be based upon the cost of acquiring properties, real assets, a reasonable amount for future development, and legitimate profits to promoters.
5.	Capitalization should be such as to enable the predicted dividends to be paid even in times of moderate trade depression.
And watering stock must be prohibited.

Is this the Inspection and Sales Act as to binder twine?

This covers inspection and sale of binder twine, hides, hay and1 straw, pot and pearl ashes. There are two hide inspectors, one at Quebec and one at Montreal. There is an inspector of fish oil, C. W. We are interested in
the names of the men but what does the inspection of hides consist of? Why does the government have a man inspecting hides? What is the idea?

I think it is more for the
protection of the farmer than anybody else, to ascertain the quality of the hides, and to see that they are properly cured. I fancy it would be more in the interests of the farmer.

The farmer is selling
hides, not buying them.
Yes, but if they are not properly cured or packed, it may react on the sale of Canadian hides.

Is that
paternal legislation?

Is there any supervision to see that the farmer gets a living wage or price for the hides? I will give an example of what I saw happen within the last two years. A farmer brought a hide into town and sold it. The hide weighed fifty pounds, and he got a cent a pound for it. The buyer was in the harness business and the farmer said, " I do not want the money, I want a hame strap." The harness man said to him, " All right, the price of the strap is seventy-five cents; you will owe me twenty-five cents." And the man gave the cow hide and1 twenty-five cents for a hame strap. I do not know how many hame straps a cow hide would make, but the labour in making these straps is not very great. It is simply a buckle riveted on one end of the strap. I am anxious to see that this inspection should extend to something in the shape of equity in the dealing in hides as well as in the curing of them.

What is the nature of the
inspection of binder twine? Is it the length or weight or quality?

We have an inspector who
travels round to the factories to see that the binder twine is made of the proper quality, and I think that work is in the interest of the agriculturist.

How many binder twine
factories are there in Canada?
I think there is only one.

How many twenty years
ago?
I do not know.

Does the inspection and
grading of hay come under this vote?

Yes. I am now negotiating
with the Department of Agriculture, because I think that the inspection of hay and straw should properly come under that department, and for that reason I made the suggestion to the Minister of Agriculture.

Will the minister give me
some assurance that this transfer will be made as promptly as possible, if it is to be made; because there are a number of men in western Canada who are anxious to have something done in regard to changes in the grading of hay, and I know that this cannot be accomplished until the transfer is made. Do I understand that
the inspectors under this vote grade hay, or set the grades of hay in any part of Canada? If it does, what steps have been taken to have the printing of the French version done simultaneously with that of the English version? I agree with my hon. friend
that the French editiom of the Commercial Intelligence Journal should be published at the same time as the English version. We were handicapped last year by reason of an insufficient appropriation for this purpose. As my hon. friend knows, the publication of the French version costs considerably more than the English, and our vote being too small our staff was reduced, resulting in the delay complained of. The whole question of publication has been referred to a committee of which Mr. Speaker is the chairman, and I hope something will be done to consolidate many of the publications upon the same, subject which are at present issued from various departments. As I said before, this vote is reduced by about $60,000. Next year I hope we may be able to reduce it still further without affecting the efficiency of the service.

Will the minister tell
us what documents he is ceasing to print in order to effect this reduction?

In the Bureau of Statistics
there are about twenty publications which we feel might well be dispensed with. I have not the list at hand to-night, but I shall be very pleased to place it on the Table at any time.

How long have these
publications been printed that are being cut out?
[Mr. Doucet.J

Some of them a year, others
two years, four years, five years. It was a matter of deciding whether the utility of these pamphlets warranted the expenditure on their publication.

The government's course
has been somewhat variable on this question. The first time any item appeared corresponding to this item of printing and stationery for the Trade and Commerce department was in 1922, the amount voted then being $125,-
000.	This government then increased the vote to $145,000. Next year they increased it to $200,000.

That increase was something
over which the government had no control. As my right hon. friend knows, the census publications in 1920-21 accounted for a large portion of the increase.

That is the whole point.
It is because we are through with the census that the diminution is made. The item, had to be put in in 1921 for the 1922 census publications, and then as the census proceeded the vote had to be increased. Of course now the vote for census publications is not necessary. That is the real explanation for the decrease.

Item agreed to.
Weights and Measures inspection, including International Bureau of Weights and Measures, $300,000.
What was the revenue and the expenditure for the past year in connection with this service?

The total revenue for the year ended January 31, 1924, was $260,868.40 and the expenditure $248,082.69, without bonus, leaving a surplus of $12,785.71. The vote shows a decrease of $10,000 but there is an actual decrease of $27,000, because the advances in the civil service re-classification amount to about $17,000. Adding that to the decrease we have an actual reduction of about $27,000.

I do not follow my
hon. friend's reasoning. He may mean that the expenditure outside the salaries has decreased $27,000, but in fact the total expenditure last year was not as much as he is voting this year.
How many inspectors are there in New Brunswick, how many are full time men and how many are part time men, and what are their salaries?

The inspectors for the district of St. John are:	William Balcom, district
inspector, $2,040; H. E. White, inspector; J.
O.	Leblanc, J. A. Bernier. Then there is an inspector of petroleum for a short time in the year; his remuneration amounts to $100. The first four I named are full time men. I may say that last year the bonuses allowed to the men amounted to $22,000.
Is that bonus cut off now?
It is still in effect until the Civil Service Commission make their report.
Does this vote include the grant to the International Bureau of Weights and Measures, and what is the amount of the grant?

The usual grant of $400 is
continued. It is included in this vote.
What is the function of this bureau?
It is something similar to the bureau respecting tariffs that was referred to a moment ago, except that it deals with weights and measures.

I can understand that in the matter of tariffs it is well that we should have information from other countries, but I do not see what it matters to us how many ounces go to the pound in Belgium or how many quarts it takes to make a gallon of gin in Holland.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
They have the metric
system there.
Are we going to adopt the metric system? What benefit do we derive from this bureau? I am asking for information.

It has continued from the year
1907. If my hon. friend is particular about the location I will be glad to get details for him.

What benefit do we
derive from this bureau?

Can the minister tell
us how much of this is for. salaries of the inspectors and the staff, and how miuch for other expenses such as rent of buildings, travelling expenses, postage, stationery, fuel and so forth. The reason I ask is I want
to compare with previous years, and in previous years the vote was divided into three items, salaries, other expenses, and then this grant of $400.

The salaries of 118 officers
amounted to $160,000; contingencies, $87,000; International Bureau, $193.76 to January 31.
I presume that is the amount that was spent in connection with the vote of $400. The item of $400 for the International Bureau of Weights and Measures is to honour an international obligation.
The International Bureau was established after a conference of 19 nations in Paris in 1875. Its objects are research work in the science relating to primary standards and the perfecting of the accuracy and relation of international units of weights and measures of electricity, heat, and so forth. The Bureau has been primarily concerned with the perfection and extension of the metric system, but this is not its only interest. Exceedingly useful work has been done in establishing beyond question the absolute values of English and American standard pounds, yards, and gallons and their absolute relation to the standard kilogramme and metre. I think that answers the question of my hon. friend (Mr. Caldwell).

I would ask the minister to take a look at his notes again and see if he is right. He said the salaries last year were $160,000, and the other items collected together, fuel rent and so on, $87,000 and $193 for the Bureau. The total of that is only $247,000. Is that all that was spent?

My hon. friend perhaps did
not hear me say that Was up to January 31, 1924.
The books are complete up to the end of the year. The information to that date is valueless.

That is the expenditure that
was given me.
What does the minister really think he is doing? Is he cutting down the salaries, or are they going up? Take 1921; are we going back or gaining compared with that year?
It is entirely controlled by the Civil Service Commission. The statutory increases must be paid.

My hon. friend knows that what he has said is giving an absolutely wrong impression. I am not talking about statutory increases, because of

Supply-Trade and Commerce
course statutory increases have to go on all the time. It is perfect nonsense to say that the Civil Service Commission passed the statutes to provide for the increases; we have always had these statutory increases, and I have never heard this excuse given before by any other minister. The Civil Service Commission has absolutely nothing to do with statutory increases. That has never been calculated before by a minister wanting to show a reduction.
That is not shown.

But my hon.
friend showed it and said there was a real saving of $27,000, which was real moonshine, If my hon. friend will look at the figures -for 1920-1921 the salaries were $163,000. The next year the amount was higher, because that was our worst period of inflation; it was then $192,-
000.	But my hon. friend is right. The proportionate rate of his salaries to-day, taking the figure he gave us of $160,000 for the year, would be far greater. It is at least $212,000 on the figures supplied by my hon. friend. There is absolutely no reason for any talk of economy in this particular matter because the salaries have gone up if the minister's figures are correct. Is not the real fact, as I suggested before, that there was a change made in the schedule of charges in 1920 or 1921, and my recollection was that it was 1920? Was it not also in 1920 that the rearrangement was made of combining the departments? I think my hon. friend will find that there was an increased tariff put in, and that is shown by the greatly improved figures for the following year.

Ninety-one statutory increases
amounted to $5,025; 107 changes in classification amounted to $12,140; 5 positions filled at higher rates, $420, making a total of $17,585. If we had been carrying on as heretofore we would have had to add that much extra to the amount that was voted last year. Deduct from the total of last year's vote these statutory increases and my hon. friend will find that there is a cut of $27,000. Let me also point out that while in the main estimates my figures show an increase }f $433,741.31, when you deduct the capital expenditure that is included this year I have in actual reduction of $766,259. There is an item of $1,000,000 for an elevator at Edmonton, and an item of $200,000 for an elevator at Halifax, or $1,200,000 in those two items. Deducting these two capital expenditures that are included in the current expenditure of 
this year, I have succeeded in making an actual reduction of $766,259.

That is a first
rate way of lathering yourself up to lather yourself down. The items are charged as they always are.

We do not have them every
year through.

Were there none last year or the year before? I have no doubt my hon. friend's predecessor the Acting Minister of Finance, if he had wanted to could have made just the same kind of argument that my hon. friend has made to-night.
He could not have made that argument because it was not there.
I think it will be found there were some. Does my hon. friend say there were no individual items in the vote last year?
One.
What one?

That is a hardy annual for decorative purposes, and used whenever there is the possibility of an election. But take Edmonton, there was an item for that in last year. We will probably find some other items if we take the necessary time to go through the estimates. But what difference does it mak^? I should think my hon. friend would not want to be boasting a tremendous lot about reductions. Now, I want to get back to this vote. Was not the rearrangement made in 1920 that my hon. friend spoke about?
Rearrangement about what?
My hon. friend explained to the committee that there was a surplus which was produced as a result of a rearrangement. When was that rearrangement made?
Towards the end of December, 1923.
What rearrangement was that?
The cutting down of the staff.
To what extent?
The cutting out of publications.

We are not
worrying about that. These publications were

Supply-Trade and Commerce
cut off because the work had stopped. I made a mistake a short time ago-
I have already told my hon. friend that in many cases districts were joined and the staff reduced.

Let us get one thing at a time. My hon. friend talks about publications cut off. That has nothing to do with this vote. Publications were cut off with the census publications which stopped after the census was concluded. I made a mistake in saying my hon. friend was entitled to some credit for $60,000. I was wrong; the census looked after that, or rather after its disappearance. So far as weights and measures are concerned how many less officials have we this year than we had last?

We have 109 as against 124 in
the year 1920-21, although the service is always extended.
One hundred and nine as against 124. What was it last year?

The details of all these matters should properly be discussed under the civil government estimates. When we come to discuss them I will be able to show my hon. friend that I have made a total reduction of from 235 to 250 in this department.

My hon. friend
gave us a reason for a surplus in connection with this vote, and I am trying to find out what there is in this statement. We have now 109 men employed under vote 390; is that right?

The number of inspectors, and
others in connection with the staff, in 192021 was 124. In 1921-22, the number was 120; in 1922-23. 119; and this year, 109. Notwithstanding the fact that the service has been extended we have made a reduction of 10.
How many more machines are there? Is not a great deal of this business being done by adding machines or mechanical devices of that character?

No, there are no automatic
machines.
So we saved 10 men as a result of the re-organization made last December? Is that right?
November or December.

What other
departments came into that? What was the change that was made?

Some of the districts were
united and some-

Any offices
closed?

I think there was an office
closed, I think the one at Sherbrooke, if I remember rightly, was transferred to Montreal.

Any transfers
to other departments?
No.

The work was
continued just as it was.
All the work is being continued and is greater in volume.

I put a question last
year under this vote, and I should like the minister to tell me whether any change has been made in consequence of it? That is in regard to the inspecting of gasoline measuring pumps. When you use sudh a pump you turn a crank round so far and it is supposed to measure a gallon.

I think the regulations are
just about the same as last year.

I think the minister
last year, if I remember rightly, promised some change. I gave a good illustration at that time of how the system of measuring works out. I do not know how often these pumps are inspected, but I remember driving into a garage once to fill my tank. That tank held, I think, ten gallons of gasoline and there were already two or three gallons in it. The garage man pumped in ten gallons. I told him I did not mind paying for the extra gallon of gasoline, but I did not like to have my tank spoiled. I told him to put the measuring pump to work because there were already two or three gallons in the tank. He got a gallon measure, turned his pump on, put the gasoline into the measure and found that the tank was a little more than two thirds full. He seemed very much surprised. I do not think he intended to wilfully defraud anybody.

Has the hon. member a copy
of the regulations adopted last year? They may provide for the suggestion to which he refers.

My suggestion was that after licensing the use of these pumps an inspection should be frequently made, because anybody who has had any experience
3496	COMMONS
Supply-Trade and Commerce
with pumps knows that the valve in the pump sometimes gets out of order very quickly. Although the pump may be inspected and found perfectly right to-day, in a month from now it may be out of order and in some cases absolutely wrong. Gasoline is a very hard thing to regulate. A pump that will pump water accurately might fail to pump gasoline, because gasoline will work out through an iron tank frequently. It certainly will work out through a wooden barrel. I urged last year very strongly that these devices for measuring gasoline should not be licensed without-
You want the measuring made visible?
Exactly.

I may say to my hon. friend
that I think the order in council that was passed in April this year contained such a provision as he speaks of. I think that feature is provided for in the new regulations.

You have not a copy
with you?

I would be very glad to send
the hon. member a copy of the regulations. I think he will find: they contain such a clause.

I will admit this pump is a very handy device; I think it saves a lot of labour. I should like to make a suggestion to the minister along the lines of what should be done. I do not think it will be necessary to do away with these pumps entirely. I think he should insist that there should be a glass receptacle that will hold a gallon of gasoline so that the gasoline might be visible as it flows into the tank.

I think some
of them work that way now.

We do not have them in the East, we are still using the old kind.
I think the department should insist that if a license is granted to a pump of this type it should have a visible addition of the kind I have mentioned.
The minister has not yet told me whether there was any increase in 1921 in the rate of fees charged.

None since I came into the
lepartment.
, I know that, but the minister has been there only a very short time.

The Minister of Trade and
Commerce does not recall that there was any change.

Was there a
change in 1920 or 1921?

I think my hon. friend will
know.
There is a sharp betterment according to the figures read by my hon. friend for 1921-22, and I think the reason was an increase in the fees.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: Was it the late government?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: Did they increase the fees?
Yes. There was an increase in efficiency also, which is sadly lacking to-day.

Item agreed to.
West India cable, $19,466.57.
Is this for repairs?

The vote last year amounted
to $29,199. This covers a period up to the 30th of September. At that time the contract was under the Post OfSce Department. At present most of these cable companies are under that department. It was thought well to transfer this to the service. Shortly after this agreement was signed war broke out and the company's operating expenses consequently increased in a manner not contemplated when the agreement was signed. The company's financial condition was carefully looked into by the Canadian High , Commissioner in London in 1921, and he reported that their position was precarious and not likely to change materially during the remaining years of the contract. Last year we had a communication from the British government stating it was the intention to build a new cable and they asked the Dominion government if they would participate in the cost. They sent forward a figure, our portion of which would exceed the amount we had been paying. I cabled back to our High Commissioner stating we were ready to contribute as long as the amount was not in excess of the amount we had been paying for a number of years. Tenders had been called for some time ago which showed a very much increased amount, and I suggested to the members of the Imperial conference when they were going

Supply-Trade and Commerce
over-the Prime Minister and other members of the government-that they should point out to the British members of the board that new tenders should be called in order to see if the price would not be reduced, with the result that I think there will be a saving to this country. In the amount which was first suggested by the British government according to the tender they had received, there was not. As the result of my cable asking assurance of no increase the British government re-examined their tender. There will now be a saving of from $16,000 to $20,000 in which Canada will share.

Will we have
an interest in this cable?
Yes.

We have a proprietary
and contractural interest in the cable, if my memory serves me right, and the whole thing is based on a contract which extends over a number of years, and which fixes our liability and also our rights, and I well recall that the condition was improving for us year by year. We had a certain amount to pay, but we had an interest in profits, and I am satisfied from memory that a large sum was coming about the time we left office. I would like to know how that has worked out. The venture was proving very successful, and the Canadian interest improved considerably.

It was found that the cable would have to be renewed, and when the Prime Minister went to London last year, I pointed out to him that tenders had been called for. The matter was taken up by the Prime Minister in London last November, and he expressed the final consent of the Canadian government to the scheme stating that drafts of the proposed legislation in the British parliament as to the final scheme and powers of the Pacific Cable Board were satisfactory. That was the cable received from London, I might say. The Minister of Trade and Commerce replied by cable to the Prime Minister in London agreeing to the proposed arrangement, providing that the cost of the subsidy to be paid would not be in excess of that now paid for the service. That cable I addressed to the Canadian Prime Minister in London. The proposal is not that Canada should pay a subsidy, but that she should assume her share of the annual deficit which would be considerably less than the subsidy paid at the present time. The Pacific Cable Board will construct and operate the new system which is expected to be ready by
October first, when the West Indies and Panama Telegraph Company will go out of business. Canada's interest in regard to the Pacific cable is looked after by the Post Office Department and Canada's representative on the board reports to that department from time to time. The Minister of Trade and Commerce has accordingly written to the Postmaster General asking if this department will take over Canada's share of this service from October first, 1924.

I do not know whether the minister has the date of it, but I would like to get if possible the contractual relationship, not in detail but in the large-the main features of it. I think we have a contractual interest in it, and there were expectations, if I could not use a stronger word, that we should not be paying half of what we were paying before, but rather by this time we should be getting a revenue. I am only making this statement as a matter or recollection, and I should like to get the facts.
The minister is right about that.

The minister is right on one point, I know that; nor do I say that any part of what he has read1 is wrong. The reason for the reduction by half this year of what it was last year is simply because the contract expires in a half year.
I explained that to the committee.
I did not get the explanation. The minister was trying to impress the committee at first that it was due to some arrangement which the Prime Minister had made in England.

No, I explained that this
covered only to the 30th of September of this year. I said that.

Supply-Trade and Commerce

The minister said that
the last time.

I also said that it accounted
for the vote being so small this year.

The minister says that
the expenses have been going up; but I noticed that the amount voted was, as I expected, exactly the same to a cent. Every year as far back as I can trace the estimate -ias far back as 1918-it has been exactly the same. This year it is just half as much, to a cent.

How does the hon. member
figure out that it is just half?
The amount before was $38,933.33 and this year it is $19,466.67.
But that is for the half year.

Yes, of course it is for
the half year, and1 this is in pursuance of the contract. There has been no extra expense year by year, or at any rate none has been yet revealed. The minister however spoke about its costing more each year.

I said it was gradually increasing. For example, in 1919-20 it was $33,723; in 1920-21 $34,066; in 1921-22 $38,917 and in 1922-23 a little larger. Probably this year it will go up slightly. My hon, friend said that it should1 be a profitable investment by this time but it has not turned out that way so far as money goes.

The amount voted every year has been the same to a cent up to this year, when for half the year it is exactly half the annual amount. It does not seem reasonable that if we were only estimating the amount we should estimate it to the accuracy of a penny.
We do that in most departments; we always estimate a little more than we spend.

But you estimate in
round figures, in hundreds or thousands.

This probably was based on
a contract.

Yes, of course; it is
based on a contract and we are paying the same amount each year. I will not press the point further. Will the minister answer this: What will happen after October? Does the contract fully expire? Have we no rights from October 1 on and if we have, what has the department in contemplation as respects this cable?
fMr. Low.]
The British government expects to build a new cable.

What are we going to
do about the matter?

We shall pay this amount to
the British government.

We shall continue the
same payment?

As I have said, there may be
a slight increase.

We are going to pay on
the same basis after October 1 as before?
Yes, I insisted that it should not be higher.

I am disappointed that
it is not a great deal lower.
How does my hon. friend expect it to be lower when it is going up a little?

Because the earnings of
the cable have been far greater. I know it was expected that we should get a profit soon.

My hon. friend knows that the
company is in bad condition financially.

I did not know it. Is
that the case?
Yes.

Has the government
ever got any revenue from the cable?
No.
Has the British government accepted the offer of the minister that we shall pay the same in future as we have done in the past?
Yes, I think they have accepted it.

I understand that at
the end of September, 1924, the service will be handed over to the Post Office Department and a vote will be provided in their estimate.
Yes, there will be an item there to cover the rest of the year.
This is not really a saving but a transfer.

There is no saving. I stated
at the outset that this would cover the period to September 30, 1924, when the matter would be transferred to the Post Office Department and a further vote would appear.

Item agreed to.

Supply-Trade and Commerce
Amount required to recoup A. E. Bryan, $4,000.
Who is Mr. Bryan, and why should he get $4,000?	_

Mr. Bryan is our trade representative in Japan. He lost all his household effects during the earthquake, and he asked the department to allow him a certain amount to recoup his loss. He presented a bill for 13,575 yen.

A yen is 50
cents.
At the time that was equivalent to about $6,786. I thought we should at least do something to compensate him and I suggested this amount of $4,000.

Item agreed to.
Miscellaneous-Patent Record, $35,000.

Mr. Chairman, we were
here last night until a quarter past one, the night before until ten minutes to one, and the night before that until about twelve twenty-five. The minister should not carry us into something else to-night.

It is only eleven o'clock
now.

There are not many items in
the patent vote.

Is the minister not
going to adopt the suggestion which I made? It is a good deal earlier than usual I know, but it is after the hour which the Prime Minister set as a reasonable hour for adjournment. We have not gone on very fast,-
We certainly have not.

-but the delay has
not been here.

I certainly have taken more
time with my estimates than I expected. However, I am not complaining. But we are all very anxious to get through with the work of the session, and I think an hour or so more would not be wasted in passing the estimates of the Patent branch.

It is all right for the
minister, when he gets his estimates through he is done; but we have to sit here and watch every item.
I am never done.

We do not want to be
imposed on. We have been very reasonable with the minister. Every time when we went past eleven o'clock with our estimates a terrible row was raised.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
In this connection there
is a consideration that perhaps will appeal to my right hon. friend the leader of the opposition. The Minister of Trade and Commerce is a member of the Redistribution committee, and the province of Ontario is now under consideration by a sub-committee of which he is a member. I am informed that this sub-committee expect within three or four days to be able to present a unanimous report to the whole committee The idea of proceeding further to-night is to enable my hon. friend to take up his work on the sub-committee next week.

Tt would seem to me
that if the minister is engaged on that work it is strange that his bill's and his estimates should have been before us continuously during the last three days.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
The hon. member felt
that he would be a good deal more at ease with his work on the Redistribution committee if he had his estimates disposed of.

He has been
furthering its work by keeping away from it for the last two or three days. I appreciate the point.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
But he expected to get
through with his estimates a good deal earlier. We do not complain; it is nobody's fault in particular, only reasonable and regular information having been asked for by hon. members and supplied by the minister. As I have said, he is anxious to get through with bis estimates in order to devote his time for the first two or three days of next week to the consideration of the readjustment in Ontario.

I think in view of the
fact that we are not yet sitting Saturdays we might very well go on for another hour. I cannot believe the right hon. leader of the opposition is serious when he says there was fault found if he went past eleven o'clock when he was in charge of the administration, because I sat here for two sessions while he was in power and' I think I am safe in saying that I never remember the House adjourning at eleven o'clock. Indeed, I have seen new estimates brought down after twelve o'clock and discussed for two hours. He should not object- very strenuously, especially towards the end of the session. We are all anxious to get through some time this summer, and if the right hon. gentleman would not object too strenuously it seems to me we might dis-

Supply-Trade and Commerce
pose of some of these estimates. To-morrow is Saturday, and we can very well afford to sit until twelve o'clock to-night.

It is perfectly true that we did sit after eleven, often after twelve o'clock, but we never did it with the acquiescence of the opposition and were always met with a row. And what is more, we were met with something altogether different from the reception which we have given these estimates. If the minister would have some one in front to supply him with information it would very much expedite progress; no minister can hunt up information with the detail required without creating serious delay. Then we devoted an hour or two to-day and an hour or two yesterday to another bill of the minister's, and nobody in this House would suggest that the delay was the fault of any member on this side. I do not think it would be necessary for me to suggest whose fault it was. Then why should we, who sat la3t night until one o'clock and who have committees every morning, be called upon to go through that process every night? It is unreasonable, it is irrational, and it does not conduce to the expeditious conduct of business.

My right hon. friend is quite
right, we have been working overtime and have done fairly well. My hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce recognizes that. He suggests that we might put through this Patent Record item, and then adjourn.

If we can get
that through without any explanation, I would let it go.

When this item was up
last session I think the minister told me that the fees charged took care of the expenses. Is that the fact?

The item amounts to $35,000
and has been reduced by $10,000. The expenditure for 1922-23 was $36,397.20; for the current year to February 29, 1924, it amounted to $31,365. The Patent Record is a publication issued pursuant to section 60 of the Patent Act. It appears every Tuesday, which is the only day that patents are issued. It gives to the public a brief description of every patent on the day it is issued. This is useful in enabling the public in general and inventors in particular to ascertain what inventions are covered by patents without the trouble of visiting the patent office. One thousand copies are printed, the distribution being as follows: subscribers, 364; exchanges, 48; free list, libraries, 231; government, 106. It is sent out only

to those on the free list who have expressed a wish to receive it. The annual subscription is $4 and the price of a single copy is 10 cents. The amount received last year from subscriptions and the sale of single copies was $1,859.19.
What is being cut out to effect the reduction?
It is economy in service.
What answer is that?

It may not suit my right hon.
friend, nevertheless it is true.

What information does
one get from that? This is why there is delay and why we are kept here all hours of the night. I asked, what is cut out? Are there men cut out? Is some part of the publication cut out? The answer I get is that there is economy in the service.
Mr. LOW':	There has been a reduction of
about thirty in the staff. The temporaries were retired first and some were retired under the Ca'lder Act.

Are the patents issued
fewer now?
I do not think so. It does not necessarily follow that fewer mien will not do the same amount of work.

I notice that previous
to 1921 it was $61,000 and that it was then cut to $45,000. Some different system must be adopted and I -would like to know what it is. Apparently under the late government there was a reduction of $16,000; now the reduction is $10,000.

There is quite a reduction in
the staff.
This is in connection with records-do not mix them.

A number of clerks are paid
out of this vote. The permanent staff and the temporary staff amount to 84 to-day as against 114 on the first of April, 1923. For salaries last year there was voted $177,000; this year we ask for $149,000. For contingencies last year we asked for $35,000 and this year $30,000. The Patent Record cost $45,000 .last year and this year it has been reduced to $35,000.

Now we will come back and see if we can get the information, though I am really not very hopeful. This is the

Postal Employees
Patent Record. The minister talked all round the bush about the employees of his department in the Patents branch, which has nothing to do with it. We tried to tell him that it had nothing to do with it, but he persisted. If the cost of publishing the Patent Record is less, there must be a reason for it. Perhaps the reason is that it is smaller, that the patents issued are fewer, that the information given is less, or that the cost of printing is less. I have asked which it is and I have been given all sorts of talk about something that does not pertain to it at all. I cannot get an answer to the simple question.

Well, a reduction has been
made in the issuing of the Patent Record, we will agree upon that. As to the details of how it is arrived at, if my right hon. friend wishes this item to stand over I will get the information for him to-morrow, or perhaps he will accept my word that I will get it, and in the meantime allow the item to go through.

Well, we will let the
item go through, so far as I am concerned, if the minister will get the information for to-morrow?

Item agreed to.
Progress reported.
